title: Moby Dick
author: Herman Melville
description: Ishmael joins the whaling ship Pequod, whose captain, Ahab, wants only one thing: to kill the white whale that took his leg.

paragraphs.t: This is the complete story of Moby Dick by Herman Melville (1851), retold in English at level B1. The original has 135 chapters and an epilogue. Here they are grouped into 33 parts. Every event of the story is included. The chapters where Melville stops the story to write about whales, ships and whaling are shortened into a few paragraphs, so that you can still learn what he wanted to tell you.
The story is told by a young sailor called Ishmael. Tap any word to see its meaning. Tap a marked phrase to see a grammar note.
The main characters
Ishmael — a young American who goes to sea on a whaling ship; he tells the story
Queequeg — a harpooner from an island in the South Pacific; Ishmael's best friend
Captain Ahab — the captain of the Pequod; he lost a leg to the white whale
Starbuck — the first mate; serious, brave and religious
Stubb — the second mate; always calm and smoking his pipe
Flask — the third mate; short and aggressive
Tashtego — a Native American harpooner, from Gay Head
Daggoo — an enormous African harpooner
Fedallah — a mysterious man from Asia, Ahab's secret harpooner
Pip — a young African-American cabin boy
Moby Dick — a huge white sperm whale, famous among all whalemen
The ship

The Pequod is an old whaling ship from Nantucket, an island near the coast of Massachusetts, in the United States. In the 1840s, American ships sailed all over the world for three or four years at a time to hunt sperm whales. The men cut the fat from the whales and boiled it on the ship to make oil, which people used in their lamps.

Call me Ishmael. Some years ago — it doesn't matter exactly how many — I had little or no money in my pocket, and nothing in particular interested me on land. So I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.

This is what I do when I feel sad and grey inside. When I find myself walking slowly past funeral shops, or following every funeral I meet in the street, or when I want to go out and knock people's hats off, then I know it is time to go to sea again. It is my way of getting rid of bad feelings. Many people feel the same way, even if they don't know it. Almost every man, at some time in his life, has the same feelings towards the ocean as I have.

Look at New York on a Sunday afternoon. Thousands of men stand along the edges of the city, looking out at the water. They work all week in offices and shops, behind desks and counters, and now they come to the sea, as close as they can get without falling in. Why? Nobody knows. But water and deep thinking go together. If you put a man who is dreaming in any place in the country, his feet will carry him to water, if there is any water in that area. Perhaps we see in the water a picture of ourselves, which we cannot catch.

When I go to sea, I never go as a passenger. Passengers must pay, and they often get seasick and argue all the time. I never go as a captain or a cook, either. I go as a simple sailor. Yes, they give me orders, and they make me jump from one end of the ship to the other. At first that hurts my pride. But who is not a slave in some way? Everybody has to obey someone. And there is one big difference between a passenger and a sailor: the sailor gets paid. Besides, the fresh wind is good for the health.

But why, after sailing many times on merchant ships, did I decide this time to go on a whaling voyage? I don't really know. Perhaps it was part of a big plan made by the Fates long ago. Perhaps it was the great whale himself. I had always wanted to see this huge and mysterious monster. I wanted to see the wild seas where he rolls his island-sized body, and the far-away places where he lives. I love to sail on forbidden seas and land on wild coasts. So the great gates of the wonder-world swung open, and in my imagination I saw endless lines of whales swimming into my soul, two by two, and in the middle of them one grand hooded ghost, like a snow hill in the air.
The Carpet-Bag

I put a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, put it under my arm, and started for Cape Horn and the Pacific. I left the old city of Manhattan and arrived in New Bedford on a Saturday night in December. I was disappointed to learn that the little boat to Nantucket had already left, and that there would be no way to get there until Monday.

Most young men who want to go whaling stop at New Bedford and sail from there. But I had decided to sail only from Nantucket, because it is the oldest and most famous whaling town in America. There was something about the place that pleased me. So I had to find somewhere to sleep for two nights in New Bedford.

It was a very dark and cold night. I had only a little money. I walked through the empty streets, looking for a cheap inn. The first two places I found looked too expensive and too happy. I could hear people laughing and singing inside. "No," I said to myself, "these are too good for me." I walked on towards the water, where the buildings looked poorer.

At one point I stumbled over a box of ashes in a doorway, and I almost fell into a building where there was a loud meeting going on. Inside, a black preacher was speaking to a black congregation about the blackness of darkness, and the weeping and wailing there. I quickly left.
At last I saw a weak light near the docks. Over the door there was an old sign with a picture of a tall, straight jet of spray, and these words: The Spouter Inn: Peter Coffin.

"Coffin?" I thought. "Spouter? That's not very cheerful. But Coffin is a common name in Nantucket, I believe, and the place looks cheap enough." The house was old and leaning, as if it were sick. The wind howled around it. It looked like the right sort of place for me.
The Spouter Inn

When I went in, I found myself in a wide, low entrance hall with old wooden walls, like those of an ancient ship. On one wall hung a very large, very dark oil painting. It was so covered with smoke and dirt that at first I could not understand what it showed. I looked at it for a long time from different sides. In the middle there was a long, black shape, floating in a grey storm. After a while I decided that it was a ship in a terrible storm, half sunk, with only its three masts showing, and a great whale jumping over it, about to land on the ship and break it in pieces.

On the opposite wall there were many strange weapons: clubs and spears from the South Sea islands, with teeth and hair on them. There were also old, rusty whaling lances and harpoons, bent and broken. Some of them had killed many whales, the landlord told me later.
At the end of the hall there was a bar, made in the shape of a whale's huge jaw. Behind it a small, old man, the landlord, was selling drinks to sailors at very high prices.

I asked him for a room. He looked at me and said that the house was full — not a single bed was free. "But wait," he added, scratching his head. "You don't mind sharing a bed with a harpooner, do you? I suppose you're going whaling, so you'd better get used to that sort of thing."

I told him that I did not like the idea of sleeping with another man. If I had to share a bed, it depended on who the harpooner was. If there really was no other place, and the harpooner was not too bad, then perhaps I would accept.
"I thought so," said the landlord. "Now sit down. Supper will be ready soon."

At supper, I ate with a group of sailors. They were quiet and almost shy, although they had just returned from a long voyage. I watched them, but there was no harpooner among them. When I asked the landlord where my bedfellow was, he only smiled in a strange way.
"Oh, he's out," he said. "He's usually back early, but tonight he's late. He's out selling his head."
"Selling his head?" I said. "What do you mean? Are you telling me that this harpooner is walking around the town on a Saturday night, trying to sell his head?"
"That's exactly what he's doing," said the landlord. "I told him he couldn't sell it here, because the market's full of them."
"Full of what?"
"Heads, of course. Aren't there too many heads in the world?"
I became angry. "Landlord," I said, "stop telling me stories. I'm not a fool."

"Calm down," he said. "This harpooner has just come from the South Seas. He bought a lot of dried and preserved heads there, from the islanders. They're very interesting things, and people like to buy them as curiosities. He has sold all of them except one, and he's trying to sell that one tonight. But tomorrow is Sunday, and it wouldn't be right to sell human heads in the street when people are going to church."

This was a strange story, but it explained everything. The landlord took a candle and led me upstairs to a cold, small room with a huge bed. "There," he said. "That's the bed. It's big enough for two. Good night." And he left me.

I looked around the room. There was a strange bag on the floor, and a mat made of grass with a hole in the middle, like the ones worn by South American people. I put it on and looked at myself in the little mirror. It was heavy and smelled wet, so I quickly took it off. Then I got into bed and lay awake for a long time, thinking about the mysterious harpooner who sold heads.
At last, just as I was falling asleep, I heard heavy footsteps in the passage, and a light came under the door.

The door opened, and a man came in with a candle in one hand and a dried human head in the other. He did not look towards the bed. He put the candle on the floor in a corner and began to untie the strings of the big bag.

I wanted to see his face, but for some time he kept it turned away. When at last he turned round, I almost cried out. What a face! It was dark purple and yellow, and it was covered with black squares, like a chess board. "He must have been in a fight," I thought, "and these are terrible bruises." But then the candle showed me that they were not bruises at all. They were tattoos.

He took off his hat, and I saw that his head was completely bald, except for a small knot of hair on the top of his forehead. His bald purple head looked like a mouldy skull. If he had not been standing between me and the door, I would have run out faster than I ever ate a dinner.

Then he took off his coat and shirt, and I saw that his whole body was covered with the same squares. His back, his chest, his arms, even his legs — they were all tattooed. He was obviously some terrible savage from the South Seas, who had somehow got onto a whaling ship and arrived in this Christian country.
I was frightened, more frightened of him than I have ever been of the devil. And I could not decide what to do. Should I speak to him, or pretend to sleep?

Then he did a very strange thing. He took from his bag a little black wooden figure, a small idol with a hump on its back, exactly the colour of a three-day-old baby. He put it in the fireplace, which was empty, and lit some small pieces of wood in front of it. Then he put some biscuit on the fire and moved his hands quickly near the flames. He seemed to be offering the biscuit to his little god, and singing a kind of prayer song. All the time his face moved strangely, as if he was in pain.

When he had finished, he put the idol back in his bag, as carelessly as if it were a dead bird. Then he took his tomahawk — a kind of axe — and put it in his mouth. It was a pipe and an axe at the same time! He lit the pipe, blew out a big cloud of smoke, and then, with the axe still in his mouth, he jumped into bed beside me.
I screamed. He gave a cry of surprise and began to feel me with his hands.
"Who-ee you?" he shouted. "You no speak-ee, damn-me, I kill-ee." And he waved the burning tomahawk over my head in the dark.
"Landlord! Help! Coffin! Angels! Save me!" I shouted.
"Speak-ee! Tell-ee me who-ee you, or damn-me, I kill-ee!" he growled again, and the hot ashes from his pipe fell all around me.
Luckily, the landlord came in with a light, and I jumped out of bed and ran to him.
"Don't be afraid," said the landlord, smiling. "Queequeg here wouldn't hurt a hair of your head."
"Stop smiling!" I shouted. "Why didn't you tell me that this harpooner was a cannibal?"
"I thought you knew. Didn't I tell you he was selling heads in the town? But go to bed again. Queequeg, you know me, and I know you. This man sleeps with you. You understand?"
"Me understand plenty," said Queequeg, and he sat up in bed, smoking his pipe.

"You get in," he added, pointing to me with his tomahawk, and moving to one side of the bed. He did it in a very polite, kind way. I stood looking at him for a moment. For all his tattooing, he was a clean, nice-looking cannibal. "Why have I been making such a noise?" I thought. "The man is a human being just as I am. He has as much reason to be afraid of me as I have to be afraid of him. Better to sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian."
"Landlord," I said, "tell him to put away his tomahawk, or pipe, or whatever it is. Tell him to stop smoking. I don't like a man smoking in bed with me. It's dangerous."

Queequeg understood at once, and he put out his pipe. Then he politely signed to me to get into bed. He moved right to the side, as if to say: "I won't touch even a leg of yours." I got into bed, and I never slept better in my life.
Morning

When I woke up the next morning, Queequeg's arm was lying over me in the most loving and affectionate manner. You would have thought I was his wife. The arm was tattooed all over with an endless pattern, and the blanket we were lying under was made of many small squares of different colours. In the morning light I could hardly tell which was his arm and which was the blanket.

I tried to move his arm away, but even in his sleep he held me tight, as though only death would part us. I called to him, but he only snored. At last, after a long time, I managed to wake him. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked at me as if he did not remember how I came to be there. Then he seemed to remember, and he jumped out of bed. He made signs to tell me that he would dress first and then leave me alone in the room to dress. It was very polite. These savages have a natural sense of good manners.

He dressed in a strange way. First he put on his tall hat. Then he crawled under the bed with his boots, and I heard him struggling and kicking there. At last he came out with the boots on. Then he washed his chest and face, and he shaved — with his harpoon! He took the long wooden pole off the iron head, sharpened the iron on his boot, and shaved his cheeks with it in front of the mirror.
Breakfast and a Walk

At breakfast, the room was full of whalemen. I had expected them to tell stories, but they were very quiet, almost shy, like sheep. Queequeg sat at the head of the table, as cool as ice. He did not use a knife or a fork. He reached across the table with his harpoon and pulled the steaks towards him with it. Nobody seemed surprised.

After breakfast I went for a walk around New Bedford. The streets were full of strange people: sailors from all over the world, cannibals, farmers who had left their fields to go whaling. The town was rich. The houses were big and beautiful, and they had all been built with money from whale oil. The wives and daughters were dressed in fine clothes. Everything there, they say, came out of the sea.
The Chapel

It was Sunday, so I went to the Whaleman's Chapel. Outside, the weather was terrible — snow and sleet. Inside, there were only a few people, mostly sailors and sailors' wives and widows. They sat apart from each other, silent, each with their own sorrow.

On the walls there were marble tablets with black borders. Each one remembered a man who had died at sea. One said: Sacred to the memory of John Talbot, who, at the age of eighteen, was lost overboard, near the Isle of Desolation, off Patagonia. Another remembered the crew of a whaleboat who had been towed out of sight by a whale and never seen again. A third remembered a captain who had been killed by a sperm whale on the coast of Japan.

I sat and read them, and I thought: "Yes, there is death in this business of whaling. A man can disappear in a moment, without a word. But so what? Perhaps I have the wrong idea about life and death. My body is only the outside of me. Anyone can take my body, but nobody can touch my soul." I was surprised to see Queequeg there among the people.
The Sermon

Then the preacher came in. His name was Father Mapple. He was a very old man, but strong, and he had been a sailor and a harpooner in his youth. The pulpit was very high, and it had no steps. Instead there was a rope ladder, like the ones on the side of a ship. Father Mapple climbed it hand over hand, like a sailor going up the mast. When he reached the top, he pulled the ladder up after him. Now he was alone in his pulpit, like a captain on his ship, far from the world.

He gave a sermon about Jonah and the whale. He told the story very simply, as one sailor to another. God told Jonah to go to the city of Nineveh and preach against the sins of the people. But Jonah did not want to obey. He tried to run away from God. He went to the port of Joppa and paid for a passage on a ship going to Tarshish, at the other end of the world.

But you cannot run away from God. A great storm came, and the ship was in danger of sinking. The sailors were afraid. They threw lots to find out who was guilty, and the lot fell on Jonah. Jonah told them: "Throw me into the sea, and the storm will stop." They did, and the storm stopped at once. Then a great whale swallowed Jonah, and he was inside it for three days and three nights. There, in the darkness, Jonah prayed to God. He did not ask to be saved; he accepted his punishment. And God made the whale throw him up onto dry land. Then Jonah went to Nineveh and preached the truth, as God had told him.

"Shipmates," said Father Mapple at the end, "this is the lesson. To obey God, we must disobey ourselves. Woe to him who tries to please men rather than to tell them the truth! But joy to him who stands up for God against the proud gods of this earth, and who remains true to God, even if the world is against him."
A Friend

When I returned to the inn, Queequeg was sitting alone by the fire. He was holding his little idol, and he was carefully counting the pages of a big book. He counted fifty pages, then stopped and gave a long whistle of surprise. Then he counted another fifty, and whistled again. It seemed he could only count to fifty, and each time he was amazed at the number of pages.

I sat and watched him. Although he was a savage with a terrible face, there was something noble in him. He had a calm, simple dignity. You cannot hide a soul, I thought. Through all his tattoos, I could see an honest heart. In his large, deep eyes there were signs of a spirit that would dare a thousand devils.

I moved my chair closer to him and tried to talk. At first he did not answer, but after a while we were speaking quite easily. Then we smoked his tomahawk pipe together, passing it from one to the other. When we had finished, he pressed his forehead against mine, put his arm around me, and said that from now on we were married. In his country, that meant that we were best friends, and that he would die for me if necessary.

After supper, he gave me the head that he had not sold, and he divided his money — about thirty dollars — into two equal parts. He pushed one part towards me and said, "Yours." I tried to refuse, but he put it in my pocket.

Then he wanted to say his evening prayers to his idol, Yojo. He invited me to join him. I am a good Christian, born and raised in the Presbyterian Church. How could I worship his little piece of wood? But then I thought: "What is worship? To do the will of God. And what is the will of God? To do to my fellow man what I would have my fellow man do to me. Queequeg is my fellow man. I would like him to join me in my worship. So I must join him in his." So I helped him light the little fire, offered biscuit to Yojo, and bowed down to the idol two or three times. Then we went to bed, at peace with our own consciences and with all the world.
Queequeg's Story

In bed, we talked for a long time. Queequeg told me about his life. He was born on an island called Kokovoko, far away in the west and south. It is not on any map; true places never are. His father was a king, and his uncle a high priest. But Queequeg was not satisfied with his island. He wanted to see the Christian world and learn its ways, so that he could make his own people happier and better.

When a whaling ship visited his island, he asked to join it. The captain refused. So Queequeg took his canoe and paddled out to a narrow passage the ship had to pass through. When the ship came, he jumped onto it, grabbed a chain and held on. The captain threatened to throw him into the sea, but Queequeg did not let go. He said they could cut off his hands, but he would not leave the ship. At last the captain, admiring his courage, let him stay.

But in the Christian world, Queequeg soon learned that Christians could be even worse than his own people. He saw sailors in the ports who were drunk and wicked. "It's a wicked world in all places," he thought. "I'll die a pagan." Now he was ashamed to go home, because he felt that the Christian ways had made him unfit to become king of his people. "But I will go home one day," he told me, "when I feel baptized again."

I told him that I planned to go to Nantucket and find a ship for a whaling voyage. He said that he would come with me. We would sail on the same ship, eat at the same table, and share the same dangers. I was very happy, because Queequeg was an experienced harpooner, and I knew almost nothing about whaling.

On Monday morning, we put our bags in a wheelbarrow and pushed it down to the harbour. People in the street stared at us — not so much at Queequeg, because they were used to seeing cannibals there, but at the two of us together, walking like old friends.

Queequeg told me a funny story about the first time he saw a wheelbarrow. In New Bedford, someone lent him one to carry his bag. He did not know how to use it. So he put the bag in the wheelbarrow, tied it tight, then lifted the whole wheelbarrow onto his shoulders and carried it up the street. Everyone laughed at him.

"But the white men," Queequeg said, "they do stupid things too." He told me about a white sea captain who came to a great feast on his island. In front of everyone, the captain washed his hands in the sacred bowl of coconut milk, thinking it was a bowl of water for washing. "What you think now?" said Queequeg. "Didn't our people laugh?"
The Little Ship

We got on a small sailing ship called the Moss, which carried passengers to Nantucket. As soon as we were out of the harbour, the ship began to dance on the waves, and I felt wonderfully happy. The wind was fresh, and the sea was blue.

But some of the young men on board were laughing at Queequeg. One of them, a country boy, stood behind him and made faces, imitating him. Queequeg turned round and saw him. He put down his harpoon, took the boy in his strong arms, and threw him high into the air. The boy turned over once and landed on his feet, very surprised but not hurt.
The boy ran to the captain. "Captain! Captain! Here's the devil!"
The captain came to Queequeg, very angry. "What do you mean by that? Don't you know you might have killed that boy?"
"What him say?" Queequeg asked me.
"He says you might have killed that man there," I said.
"Kill-ee?" said Queequeg, and his face showed a strange, scornful look. "Ah! Him small-ee fish. Queequeg no kill-ee so small-ee fish. Queequeg kill-ee big whale!"
"Listen," said the captain. "I'll kill-ee you, you cannibal, if you play any more of your tricks on board here. So mind yourself."

But just then, something terrible happened. The strong wind had broken the rope that held the great boom — the heavy wooden pole at the bottom of the mainsail. The boom was swinging from side to side across the back of the ship, knocking everything over. Suddenly it hit the country boy who had mocked Queequeg, and threw him into the sea.

Everyone was frightened. Nobody knew what to do. But Queequeg acted at once. He fell on his knees, crawled under the swinging boom, caught the end of a rope, and tied it fast to the ship. When the boom stopped swinging, he took off his shirt and jumped into the cold sea.

For three minutes or more, he swam like a dog, looking for the boy, throwing his long arms forward. The boy had disappeared below the water. At last Queequeg dived down, and after a moment he came up again, with one arm still swimming and the other holding a lifeless body. They pulled them on board. The poor boy came back to life, and all the passengers said that Queequeg was a hero. The captain apologised to him.

But Queequeg did not seem to think he had done anything special. He only asked for some fresh water to wash off the salt, then put on dry clothes, lit his pipe, and leaned against the side of the ship, looking calmly at the people around him. He seemed to be thinking: "It's a mutual world, all over. We cannibals must help these Christians."
Nantucket

Nantucket is a small island far out in the Atlantic. Look at it on a map. It is nothing but sand — no trees, no grass, just a hill of sand. People joke that the people of Nantucket have to bring wood from the mainland to make fires, and that they plant mushrooms between the stones because nothing else will grow.

But this little island is the centre of the whaling world. The people of Nantucket began by catching crabs and fish on the beach. Then they went out in small boats to catch whales near the coast. Then they built bigger ships, and went further and further, until they had sailed over all the oceans of the world. Now the sea belongs to them, as the land belongs to the emperors. The Nantucketer lives on the sea, as the prairie dog lives on the prairie. He hides among the waves; he climbs them as hunters climb the Alps. For years he sees no land. When he comes home at last, the land smells strange to him, as the moon would smell to a man from the earth. He sleeps with the noise of the waves in his ears, and dreams of whales.
The Try Pots

It was quite late in the evening when we arrived at Nantucket. Before we left New Bedford, Peter Coffin had told me about an inn there, run by his cousin Hosea Hussey. "There's no better place in the world for chowder," he said. So we looked for it.

After some time, we found it. At the door, there were two big black pots hanging from the branches of an old mast, like the ones used on whaling ships to boil the fat into oil. That is why the inn was called the Try Pots. The pots looked a bit like gallows, which did not seem a very good sign. But we went in.
Mrs Hussey, a woman with a loud voice and a red face, met us at the door. Her husband was away. "Clam or cod?" she asked us immediately.
"What's that about cods, ma'am?" I asked politely.
"Clam or cod?" she repeated.
"A clam for supper? A cold clam? Is that what you mean, Mrs Hussey?" I said. "Isn't that a rather cold and wet welcome in the winter?"
But she was in a hurry, and she only shouted "Clam for two!" towards the kitchen and disappeared.

Queequeg and I sat down to wait. Soon a delicious smell came from the kitchen, and two steaming bowls of chowder arrived. Oh, my friends! It was made of small, juicy clams, mixed with crushed biscuit and salted pork, with plenty of butter, salt and pepper. We were very hungry after our journey, and we ate it quickly. Then I had an idea. I went to the kitchen door and said, "Cod," and waited. A few minutes later we had two bowls of cod chowder, just as good as the first.

Everything at the Try Pots was chowder. Chowder for breakfast, chowder for dinner, chowder for supper, until you began to look for fish bones in your clothes. The milk tasted of fish, and even the cows, they said, were fed on fish heads.

When we went up to our room, Mrs Hussey stopped us and took Queequeg's harpoon away. "No harpoons in the rooms," she said. "Ever since a young man was found dead in Number Three, with a harpoon in his side. Now go to bed, both of you."

The next morning, Queequeg told me something important. He had talked to Yojo, his little god, about which whaling ship we should join. Yojo had said that I should choose the ship myself — alone. Yojo had already decided which ship it would be, Queequeg said, and if I let myself be guided, I would find it by accident.
So, while Queequeg stayed in our room for a day of fasting and prayer, I went down to the harbour alone to look for our ship.

There were three ships in the harbour that were getting ready for three-year voyages: the Devil-Dam, the Tit-bit and the Pequod. I looked at the Devil-Dam and the Tit-bit, but they did not please me. Then I went on board the Pequod, and I knew at once that this was the ship for us.

The Pequod was named after a Native American tribe from Massachusetts, a tribe that no longer exists. She was a small, old ship, with an old-fashioned shape. Her sides had been darkened by the weather of all four oceans. Her old masts had been cut in Japan, after the original ones had been lost in a storm. Her decks were worn like an old church floor where many pilgrims have walked.

But the strangest thing about her was her decoration. All around her sides, instead of wood, there were long, sharp teeth of sperm whales, used like pegs to hold the ropes. Her tiller — the handle used to steer the ship — was not made of wood but of the long, thin lower jaw of a whale. She was a cannibal of a ship, decorated with the bones of her enemies.

I looked around for someone in charge. Near the main mast there was a strange little tent, made of long pieces of whalebone. Inside sat an old man, brown and strong, dressed in the old-fashioned Quaker style. He was looking at me with sharp, small eyes, wrinkled from years of looking into storms at sea.
"Is this the captain of the Pequod?" I asked.
"Suppose it is. What dost thou want with him?" he said. He spoke in the old Quaker way, using "thee" and "thou" instead of "you".
"I was thinking of shipping," I said.
"Oh, were you? I can see you are not from Nantucket. Have you ever been in a boat that a whale broke?"
"No, sir, never."
"So you know nothing at all about whaling — eh?"
"Nothing, sir. But I have been in the merchant service several times."
"Forget the merchant service! Don't talk to me about it. Why do you want to go whaling?"
I told him that I wanted to see what whaling was, and to see the world.
"Want to see what whaling is, eh? Have you seen Captain Ahab?"
"Who is Captain Ahab, sir?"
"Aye, aye, I thought so. Captain Ahab is the captain of this ship."
"I am mistaken then. I thought I was speaking to the captain himself."

"You are speaking to Captain Peleg, young man. Captain Bildad and I are the owners. We get the ship ready for her voyages. But if you want to know what whaling is, I can tell you. Look at Captain Ahab, young man, and you will see that he has only one leg."
"What do you mean, sir? Was the other one lost by a whale?"
"Lost to a whale! Young man, come closer. It was eaten, chewed up and crushed by the most monstrous whale that ever broke a boat! Ah, ah!"
I was a little frightened by his passion, but I said that I still wanted to go. So he took me to see Captain Bildad, the other owner.
Peleg and Bildad

Captain Bildad was sitting in the cabin, reading a big Bible. He was a thin, dry old man, a strict Quaker, who had made a lot of money from whaling. He had been a famous captain, and they said that he had been a very hard one, who never let his men rest. He never swore and never laughed. Peleg, on the other hand, swore all the time and did not care what anyone thought of him.

The two old captains began to discuss how much I should be paid. On a whaling ship, men do not get a salary. Each man gets a lay — a share of the profit from the oil, when the ship comes home. The captain gets a big share, the officers get smaller ones, and the simple sailors get very small ones. I expected something like the 275th lay — that means one part in 275 of all the money.
"Well, Captain Bildad," said Peleg, "what lay shall we give this young man?"

"Thou knowest best," said Bildad in a quiet voice, without looking up from his Bible. "The seven hundred and seventy-seventh wouldn't be too much, would it? The Bible says we must not keep treasures on earth..."
"Seven hundred and seventy-seventh!" I thought. That would be almost nothing!
"Damn it, Bildad!" cried Peleg. "You don't want to cheat this young man! He must have more than that. Give him the three hundredth lay."

They argued for a long time. Peleg shouted, and Bildad read his Bible and said quiet things about saving money. In the end, Peleg won, and they put me down for the three hundredth lay. I signed the papers. Then I told them that I had a friend, a harpooner, who would like to sail too. "Bring him along tomorrow," said Peleg.
Before leaving, I asked to see Captain Ahab.
"Why do you want to see him?" said Peleg. "It's all right. You are on the ship's list now."
"Yes, but I should like to see him."

"I don't think you can at the moment. I don't know exactly what's the matter with him. He stays inside his house. He is a kind of sick, and yet he doesn't look sick. Captain Ahab is a grand, ungodly, god-like man. He doesn't speak much, but when he speaks, you should listen. He has studied in colleges, and he has lived among cannibals. He has seen stranger wonders than the waves, and he has fought stranger enemies than whales."

Then he told me that Ahab had been named after a wicked king in the Bible, whose blood was licked by dogs. "But he did not choose his own name," said Peleg. "Captain Ahab is a good man — not a pious, good man, like Bildad, but a swearing good man, something like me, only there's a good deal more of him. Since he lost his leg on the last voyage, he has been a little moody — wild sometimes. But it will all pass. And remember, he has a wife — a sweet, young girl — and a little child. So he can't be completely bad."
I left the ship with strange feelings. I felt pity for Captain Ahab, and also a kind of fear. But I soon forgot him, because I had other things to think about.
Queequeg's Ramadan

Queequeg had told me that he would spend the whole day in our room, fasting and praying. It was his "Ramadan", as he called it. I did not want to disturb him, so I stayed away until the evening. But when I returned to the inn, the door of our room was locked, and he did not answer when I knocked.
"Queequeg!" I called. "Queequeg! Why don't you speak?"

Nothing. I began to be afraid. Perhaps he was ill. Perhaps he had killed himself. I ran down to Mrs Hussey, and together we came back. She had brought a hammer and an axe, and she was shouting about the young man in Number Three. I did not wait for her. I threw myself against the door with all my strength, and it burst open.

There sat Queequeg in the middle of the room, cool and calm, squatting on the floor with his legs crossed. On the top of his head sat his little idol, Yojo. He did not look at us. He did not move. He looked like a statue.
"Queequeg," I said, "what's the matter with you?"

He did not answer. Mrs Hussey went away, satisfied that he was alive. I sat down and waited for him to finish. He sat there all night, without moving or speaking, until the sun rose the next morning. Then he stood up, stiff and slow, and smiled at me as if nothing had happened.

I told him then, as gently as I could, what I thought about his Ramadan. I said that fasting for days and sitting on cold floors all night was bad for the health. It was bad for the soul, too. It gave people stomach problems and gloomy thoughts. All these religious ideas about hell, I said, were caused by bad digestion.

Queequeg listened politely, but he did not seem convinced. He only looked at me with a kind of pity, as if he thought I needed someone to save me from my own foolishness. Then we went down to breakfast, and Queequeg ate so much that Mrs Hussey worried that she would not have enough food for her other guests.

chapters.title: Part 5 — The Prophet and the Departure

paragraphs.t: When Queequeg and I went down to the Pequod together, Captain Peleg shouted from the deck that cannibals were not allowed on board unless they showed their papers.
"What do you mean?" I said. "This is Queequeg, a member of the First Congregational Church."
"Hmm," said Bildad, looking at Queequeg's tattoos. "Young man, how long has he been a member? He looks like he has not even been baptized."

I told them that Queequeg belonged to the great church of the whole world — the church to which all of us belong, Christians and pagans, because we all worship the same God in our own ways. Peleg laughed. "Young man, you'd better ship as a missionary instead of a sailor! I never heard a better sermon. But let's see if this cannibal can throw a harpoon."

Queequeg did not say a word. He picked up his harpoon and jumped onto the side of the ship. He pointed at a small drop of tar on the water, far out, and said, "You see him small drop tar on water dere? You see him? Well, spose him one whale eye, well, den!" And he threw the harpoon. It flew across the deck and hit the drop of tar exactly, making it disappear.
"Quick, Bildad!" cried Peleg. "Get the papers! We must have him. We'll give him the ninetieth lay, and that's more than any harpooner from Nantucket ever got!"

Queequeg could not write his name. So he signed the paper with a copy of a strange round shape that was tattooed on his arm. Before we left, Bildad gave him a little religious booklet called The Latter Day Coming; or No Time to Lose, and tried to talk to him about his soul. Peleg pulled him away. "Leave him alone, Bildad. Pious harpooners never make good sailors. They lose all their courage."
Elijah
As Queequeg and I were walking away from the ship, a man stopped us. He was dressed in dirty old clothes, and his face was marked by smallpox. He pointed at the Pequod with his thick finger.
"Shipmates," he said, "have you shipped in that ship?"
"Yes," I said. "We have just signed the papers."
"Anything down there about your souls?"
"About what?"

"Oh, perhaps you haven't got any," he said quickly. "No matter, though. I know many men who have no souls. Good luck to them. They are better off without them. A soul's a sort of fifth wheel to a wagon."
"What are you talking about?" I said.
"Have you seen Old Thunder?"
"Who is Old Thunder?"
"Captain Ahab."
"No, we haven't seen him yet. They say he is sick, but he is getting better."
"Getting better!" The stranger laughed strangely. "Look here. When Captain Ahab is all right, then this left arm of mine will be all right. Not before."
"What do you know about him?"

"What did they tell you about him? Did they tell you about the time he was in a fight with a Spaniard in front of an altar in Santa? Did they tell you about the time he lay like dead for three days and nights off Cape Horn? Did they tell you how he lost his leg? Ah, I see they didn't tell you everything. Well, it is all fixed now. Some sailors must go with him, I suppose. Goodbye, shipmates. May God bless you."
"Wait," I said. "If you have something important to tell us, tell us. If not, stop trying to frighten us."
"Oh, you'll find out," he said. "Goodbye." He turned away. Then he looked back and said, "Oh, I forgot. My name is Elijah." And he went away.

I told Queequeg that the man was a crazy fool, just trying to scare us. But for some reason, his strange words stayed in my mind. Elijah was the name of a prophet in the Bible — the prophet who spoke against the wicked King Ahab.
Getting Ready

For several days, there was a lot of activity on board the Pequod. Men carried on old sails, new ropes, barrels of water, bread, meat, and all the things that a ship needs for a voyage of three years. A whaling ship must carry spare boats, spare masts and spare harpoons, because she is far from any port for many months. She must carry everything a whole village would need.

Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady called Aunt Charity, was everywhere at once. She brought jars of pickles, quills for writing, a new Bible for the first mate, and a nightcap for the second mate. She ran up and down the ship all day, worrying about everyone.

But during all this time, nobody saw Captain Ahab. He stayed in his house in the town. When I asked about him, they said that he was getting better, and that he would come on board before the ship sailed.
At Dawn

On the morning we were to sail, Queequeg and I went down to the harbour very early, before the sun was up. There was a grey mist. As we came near the ship, I thought I saw some dark figures running through the mist towards the Pequod. They went on board and disappeared.
"Look, Queequeg," I said. "Are those sailors?" But when we got on board, there was nobody on deck. Everything was quiet.
At that moment, someone touched my shoulder. It was Elijah.
"Going aboard?" he asked.
"Yes. Leave us alone."
"Did you see anything like men going towards that ship a while ago?"
"Yes, I thought I saw four or five men. But it was too dark to be sure."
"Very dark, very dark," said Elijah. "Well, I wonder if you'll find them tonight. Goodbye. Goodbye. I won't stop you any longer." And he went away into the mist, laughing quietly.

We went on board. Everything was silent. In the forecastle — the room at the front of the ship where the sailors sleep — there was only an old sailor asleep on a pile of ropes. Where had the dark men gone? I never found out, at least not then.
Merry Christmas

At last, at noon on a cold, grey Christmas Day, the Pequod was ready to sail. The crew were on board. The two old owners, Peleg and Bildad, were giving orders. They would guide the ship out of the harbour and then return to land in a small boat.

There was still no sign of Captain Ahab on deck. They said he was in his cabin. I thought it was strange that a captain would not come up to watch his ship leave port. But perhaps, I thought, it was normal on whaling ships. The owners often take the ship out to sea themselves, and the captain only comes up when they have gone.

Captain Peleg shouted orders and swore at the men. Bildad sang a sad old hymn about the green fields of heaven, beyond the flood. The men sang too, as they pulled up the heavy anchor. At last the Pequod began to move. The wind was cold and strong, and the waves were rising. Snow and ice covered the ropes.

When we were outside the harbour, the two old captains got ready to leave. Bildad walked slowly up and down the deck. It was very hard for him to leave the ship, because he had put a lot of his money into her, and because he had sailed for many years himself. He looked at the sails and the ropes, and he took the hands of the officers.

"Mr Starbuck, be careful with the cask of butter. You used too much on the last voyage. And don't let the men waste the candles. And don't whale on Sundays, Mr Stubb, if you can help it. But don't miss a good chance, either. That would be rejecting Heaven's good gifts."
"Come, come, Captain Bildad," said Peleg. "Stop talking. Away!"

The two old men climbed down into their boat. They waved to us, and we gave three loud cheers. Then the Pequod turned her face to the open ocean, and we sailed out into the lonely Atlantic, like fate.

chapters.title: Part 6 — The Officers and the Harpooners

paragraphs.t: At the wheel, as we sailed away from land, I saw a tall man called Bulkington. I had first noticed him in New Bedford, at the Spouter Inn. He had just come home from a voyage of four years — and now, after only a few days on land, he was going to sea again. The land seemed to burn his feet.

I think of him as a ship in a storm that must stay far from the coast. For a ship in danger, the land is the worst enemy. The safe harbour is where the rocks are. The only safety is in the open sea. In the same way, some men cannot live in comfort and safety. They need the endless, dangerous freedom of the ocean, where the deepest truths are found. Bulkington was one of them. He does not appear again in this story, so I write about him here, like a short gravestone for a brave man.
In Defence of Whaling
Many people on land think that whaling is a dirty, low business, and that whalemen are no better than butchers. I want to say a few words against this idea.

Yes, our work is bloody. But soldiers kill too, and the world honours them. Whaling is dangerous: every whaleman risks his life many times on every voyage. And the world owes us a lot. For many years, almost every lamp and candle in the world burned whale oil. Our ships explored the unknown seas long before the navies of the world did. Whalemen found new islands and new coasts. They opened the Pacific Ocean to trade.

Whaling is also an old and noble business. In some countries, the kings used to receive the heads of whales as gifts. And if anything good is ever done by me — if I ever deserve any honour at all — then I will owe it to whaling, because a whaling ship was my college.
The Three Mates

The first mate of the Pequod was Starbuck. He was from Nantucket, and his family were Quakers. He was a tall, thin man, about thirty years old, with dry skin like old bread that has been kept a long time. He looked healthy and strong, made for long voyages and hard weather. He was a serious man, careful and religious. He did not like to take unnecessary risks.

"I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale." He meant that the most useful courage is the kind that comes from understanding the danger, not from foolishness. A man who is not afraid of a whale is a fool, and fools get killed. Starbuck was not in the ocean to kill whales for fun. He was there to make a living for his wife and child back in Nantucket. His father and his brother had both been killed by whales. He was brave, but his courage was the courage of a calm, sensible man. Later we will see that it was not strong enough against a madman.

The second mate was Stubb. He was from Cape Cod. He was always happy and relaxed, whatever happened. When a whale was near and the boats were lowered, he went into danger as calmly as a workman goes to work. He hummed songs while he fought the whale. He made jokes when death was close. And he always had a short black pipe in his mouth. He took it out only to sleep, and even then he put it next to his bed, so he could light it the moment he woke up. Perhaps the tobacco smoke kept away all the sad thoughts that most men have.

The third mate was Flask, from Tisbury, on Martha's Vineyard. He was a short, round, red-faced young man. He was very aggressive towards whales. He seemed to think that the great whales were his personal enemies, and that it was his duty to destroy them all. He felt no wonder or fear at their huge size. To him, a whale was just a kind of big mouse, or at most a water-rat. Because he was so short and strong, and because he could not be knocked down, the sailors called him "King-Post", after a short, thick piece of wood used on ships.

These three mates were the heads of three of the whaleboats. When whales were seen, each mate commanded one boat, like a captain commands a ship. And each mate had a harpooner, who was like his squire, as in the days of knights.
The Harpooners
Queequeg was chosen by Starbuck as his harpooner.

Stubb's harpooner was Tashtego, a Native American from Gay Head, on Martha's Vineyard. His people had been great hunters in the forests of New England. Tashtego had long, black, shining hair, high cheekbones and black, round eyes. Now, instead of hunting deer in the forest, he hunted whales in the sea.

Flask's harpooner was Daggoo, an enormous black man from Africa. He was six feet five inches tall — a giant. He wore two large gold rings in his ears. When he was young, he had jumped onto a whaling ship that stopped on the coast of his country, and he had been a whaleman ever since. Because Flask was so short and Daggoo was so tall, it was very funny to see them together. When Flask wanted to see far over the waves, he climbed onto Daggoo's shoulders, and Daggoo stood still and proud, like a statue, while the little man looked out from the top.
The Crew

The other men on the Pequod came from every country in the world. As on most American whaling ships, the officers were Americans, but most of the simple sailors were not. There were men from the Azores, from Ireland, from England, from Denmark, from the islands of the Pacific, from China, from India. They were all "isolatoes" — lonely men, each on his own island, without a country. But now, on the Pequod, they were all together, like a crowd of men from every nation who had come to the end of the world to stand before a judge.

And among them was little Pip, a young black boy from Alabama, who beat a small drum and danced for the crew. Poor Pip! You will hear more about him later. He was the most unimportant person on the ship, and his story is one of the saddest.

For several days after leaving Nantucket, nobody saw Captain Ahab. The three mates took turns on watch, and they gave all the orders. Sometimes they went down into the captain's cabin and came back up with orders from him, as if they were taking messages from a hidden god. I began to feel uneasy. I remembered Elijah's strange words.

The ship sailed south. The weather was still cold and grey, and the sea was rough. Then one morning, as I went up on deck for the morning watch, I looked towards the back of the ship, the part called the quarter-deck, and a shiver ran through me. Captain Ahab was standing there.

He looked like a man who has been burned alive and has not been destroyed — like a statue made of bronze. He was tall and wide, and he stood very straight. A long, thin scar ran down from his grey hair, across one side of his face and neck, and disappeared into his clothes. It looked like the mark that lightning leaves on a great tree, when it runs down the trunk without breaking it. Nobody knew if the scar went all the way down his body. An old sailor said that Ahab had been born with it. Others said he had got it in a fight at sea.

But the strangest thing about him was his leg. His real leg had been taken by a whale. Now he stood on an artificial leg made of white ivory — polished bone from the jaw of a sperm whale. On each side of the quarter-deck, there was a small hole in the wooden floor, about half an inch deep. Ahab put the end of his ivory leg into one of these holes. That kept him steady when the ship rolled. He stood there, looking straight ahead over the front of the ship, with a terrible, determined look in his eyes. He did not say a word. Nobody spoke to him. But you could see that he was suffering from some great, secret pain.

After that first morning, he came up on deck almost every day. Sometimes he stood in his hole. Sometimes he sat on a stool made of ivory. Sometimes he walked up and down the deck for hours. As the weather got warmer and we sailed into the south, his face seemed to get a little softer, like an old tree in spring. But the sad, hard look never left him for long.
Ahab and Stubb

Ahab did not sleep much. Old men often sleep very little, and Ahab slept less than any man I ever knew. At night, he often walked on the deck for hours, while the men tried to sleep below. Every step of his ivory leg on the wooden floor sounded like a hammer knocking on a coffin, and the sailors in their beds could hear it.
One night, Stubb went up to him and politely asked him if he could put something soft on the end of his ivory leg, to make it quieter.

Ahab turned round and looked at him. "Am I a cannon-ball, Stubb," he said, "that you want to wrap me in cloth? Go away. I had forgotten. Go down to your bed — your nightly grave, where men like you sleep between sheets, to get used to the coffin that will hold you one day. Down, dog, to your kennel!"
Stubb was shocked. "I am not used to being spoken to like that, sir," he said. "I don't like it at all."
"Go! Or I'll remove you from this world!" cried Ahab, and he came towards Stubb with such a terrible face that Stubb stepped back.

"Nobody ever spoke to me like that without getting a hard punch," said Stubb to himself as he went down the stairs. "It's very strange. I don't know whether to go back and hit him, or to kneel down here and pray for him. Yes, that was the thought that came into my head. But I have never prayed in my life! He's the strangest old man I ever sailed with. How his eyes burned at me! Is he mad?"

That night Stubb had a strange dream. He dreamed that Ahab kicked him with his ivory leg. When Stubb tried to kick back, his leg came off. Then a little old man with a hump on his back appeared and said, "Why do you complain? Being kicked by a great man is an honour. Old Ahab is a great man. You should be proud that he kicked you." When Stubb woke up, he told the dream to Flask. "Flask," he said, "I think the best thing is to let that old man alone. Never speak to him, whatever he says."
The Pipe
When Stubb had gone, Ahab sat down on his ivory stool and asked for his pipe. He lit it and began to smoke. But after a while, he took it out of his mouth.

"What is this?" he said to himself. "Smoking no longer calms me. Oh, my pipe! Why do I need you? A pipe is for peaceful men, for calm thoughts and soft white hair — not for torn grey hair like mine. I'll smoke no more."
And he threw the pipe, still burning, into the sea. The fire hissed in the waves. The ship sailed on, leaving it behind. Then Ahab walked away, with his hat pulled down over his eyes.
From that night, everyone on the ship felt that something was wrong. The captain was a man with a terrible secret, and sooner or later we would all know what it was.

chapters.title: Part 8 — Whales, Officers and the Mast-Head

paragraphs.t: What Is a Whale?

Before we go further, I want to say something about whales themselves. Scientists have tried for many years to put whales into groups, as they do with other animals, but nobody has done it well. The sea is so big, and the whales are so hard to see, that much is still unknown.

Some scientists say that a whale is not a fish, because it breathes air, has warm blood and feeds its babies with milk. I do not agree with them. I follow the old sailors, who say that a whale is a spouting fish with a horizontal tail. That is good enough for me.
I will divide whales into three groups, like books: large, medium and small.

The large whales are the giants. The greatest of them is the sperm whale. It is the largest animal in the world, the most dangerous to hunt, and the most valuable. Its head contains a precious oil called spermaceti, which makes the best candles. Then there is the right whale, which was hunted first by the old whalemen. It gives the long, flexible "whalebone" that ladies use in their clothes. There is the fin-back, a very fast and wild whale, which is rarely caught. There is the humpback, which is playful and often jumps out of the water. And there are others.
The medium whales include the grampus and the killer whale, which is very fierce and attacks even large whales.

Among the small whales are the porpoises, the happy fish that swim in groups in front of ships, jumping in and out of the waves. When sailors see them, they shout, "Hooray!" because they believe it means good luck.

There are also some whales that are known only from old stories. I leave them for others to study. This system of mine is not complete, and I do not think it ever will be. God keep me from ever completing anything. This whole book is only a draft — no, only the draft of a draft.
The Captain Alone

In the old days, on Dutch whaling ships, the chief harpooner was almost as important as the captain. Now that is no longer true. But on an American whaling ship, the harpooners still have special rights. They sleep and eat with the officers, at the back of the ship, not with the simple sailors at the front.

The captain is above everyone. On most whaling ships, he is friendly with his officers, and they talk and joke together. But Captain Ahab was not like that. He did not use his power to frighten people, but he kept himself completely apart. He was like the last grey bear in a forest, living alone in his cave for the whole winter, feeding on his own pain.
Dinner in the Cabin
At dinner time, the cook's boy called, "Dinner, Mr Starbuck," and then Ahab went down to his cabin. One by one, in order of rank, the officers followed him.

At the table, Ahab sat at the head, like a silent lion among his cubs. The mates waited for him to give them food, with the respect of small children. Nobody spoke. If Ahab did not speak, nobody else dared. Starbuck got his meat first, then Stubb, then Flask. Poor Flask was the last to come and the first to leave. He was always hungry. He had to wait until everyone else had their food, and he had to leave before the others finished. "Since I became an officer," he said, "I have never had a full stomach. I was much happier as a simple sailor, when I could eat as much as I wanted."

When the officers had finished, the harpooners came down to eat what was left. They were very different. They made a lot of noise, laughing and talking. They ate enormous amounts of meat. Queequeg and Tashtego cut the meat with their knives, and Daggoo took big pieces in his huge hands. The cook's boy was afraid of them, and he ran in and out as quickly as he could.
On the Mast-Head

On a whaling ship, there are always men at the top of the masts — the mast-heads — looking for whales. They stay there all day, for two hours at a time, one man after another. It is a lonely job. You stand on two small pieces of wood, a hundred feet above the deck, and the ship swings gently from side to side like a tree in the wind.

My turn came, like everyone else's. But I was a very bad lookout. In that high, quiet place, with the blue sea all around me, I forgot all about whales. I began to dream. I thought about life and death, about the soul and the universe. The waves below me became a picture of my own deep thoughts. I lost myself completely in my dreams.

This is a danger, and I warn all young men who like to think too much: be careful on the mast-head! If you forget yourself completely, you may move your foot or your hand a little, and fall. Your scream will sound for one moment in the air, and then you will drop into the sea and never come up again. So, young dreamers, keep one eye on your feet.
Whaling captains often complain about young men like me. "These dreamers come on board to think about the universe," they say, "and they never see a single whale."

One morning, soon after breakfast, Ahab came up on deck as usual. He walked up and down for a long time. His ivory leg made deep marks in the wood, and his face looked very serious. You could see that he had a fixed idea in his head, and that it was turning round and round inside him, like a wheel.
"Look at him," whispered Stubb to Flask. "The chick that's in him is pecking at the shell. It'll soon be out."
The hours passed. Then, near the end of the day, Ahab suddenly stopped beside the main mast and gave an order. "Mr Starbuck! Send everybody aft!"

Starbuck was surprised, because this order is only given on very important occasions. But he obeyed. Soon the whole crew was standing together at the back of the ship. Even the men at the mast-heads came down. They all looked at Ahab, curious and a little afraid. He looked at them for a moment. Then he shouted:
"What do you do when you see a whale, men?"
"Sing out for him!" they answered with one voice.
"Good!" cried Ahab, in a wild, happy voice. "And what do you do next, men?"
"Lower the boats, and go after him!"
"And what tune is it you pull to, men?"
"A dead whale or a broken boat!"
With every answer, Ahab's face grew more strange and full of joy. The sailors looked at each other, surprised that they were so excited by such simple questions.
Then Ahab held up a large gold coin in the sunlight. It was a Spanish doubloon, worth sixteen dollars.
"Look at this, men! Do you see this Spanish gold? It is worth sixteen dollars. Mr Starbuck, give me a hammer."

He took the hammer, and with the coin in his other hand, he walked to the main mast. "Whoever of you," he shouted, "raises me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled forehead and a crooked jaw — whoever raises me that white-headed whale, with three holes in his right tail — whoever of you raises me that same white whale, he shall have this gold coin, my boys!"
And he nailed the coin to the mast.
"Hooray! Hooray!" cried the sailors, waving their hats.
"It's a white whale, I say," continued Ahab. "A white whale. Keep your eyes open for white water. If you see even a bubble, sing out!"

All this time, Tashtego, Daggoo and Queequeg had been listening with great interest. When Ahab spoke about the wrinkled forehead and the crooked jaw, they started, as if each of them had a memory of it.
"Captain Ahab," said Tashtego, "that white whale must be the same one that some call Moby Dick."
"Moby Dick?" shouted Ahab. "Do you know the white whale, then, Tash?"
"Does he fan his tail a little strangely before he goes down, sir?" asked Tashtego.
"And has he a curious spout too," said Daggoo, "very bushy, even for a sperm whale, and very quick, Captain Ahab?"

"And he have one, two, three — oh! good many iron in him hide, too, Captain," cried Queequeg, "all twiske-tee be-twisk, like him — him —" He moved his hand round and round, trying to find the word for "corkscrew".

"Corkscrew!" cried Ahab. "Yes, Queequeg, the harpoons lie all twisted and bent in him. Yes, Daggoo, his spout is a big one, like a whole field of wheat, and white as a pile of wool. Yes, Tashtego, and he fans his tail like a broken sail in a storm. Death and devils! Men, it is Moby Dick you have seen — Moby Dick — Moby Dick!"
"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, who, with Stubb and Flask, had been looking at Ahab with growing surprise, "Captain Ahab, I have heard of Moby Dick. But wasn't it Moby Dick that took off your leg?"

"Who told you that?" cried Ahab. Then he became quiet for a moment. "Yes, Starbuck. Yes, my hearts, all of you. It was Moby Dick that took my leg. It was Moby Dick that brought me to this dead stump I stand on now." He raised his arms and shouted with a terrible, loud cry, like a wounded animal. "Yes, yes! And I'll chase him round Good Hope, and round the Horn, and round the Norway whirlpool, and round the fires of hell before I give him up. And this is what you have shipped for, men! To chase that white whale on both sides of the world, until he spouts black blood and rolls dead in the water. What do you say, men? Will you join hands on it now? I think you look brave."
"Yes, yes!" shouted the harpooners and the sailors, running closer to the excited old man. "A sharp eye for the white whale! A sharp lance for Moby Dick!"

"God bless you," Ahab said, half crying and half shouting. "Steward! Bring the drink. But what's this long face about, Mr Starbuck? Won't you chase the white whale? Aren't you brave enough for Moby Dick?"

"I am brave enough for his crooked jaw, and for the jaws of Death too, Captain Ahab, if it comes in the way of our business," said Starbuck. "But I came here to hunt whales, not my commander's revenge. How many barrels will your revenge give you, even if you get it, Captain Ahab? It will not bring much money in our Nantucket market."
"Nantucket market! Ha!" cried Ahab. "If money is your measure, man, then let me tell you that my revenge will bring a great profit — here!" And he hit his own chest.

"Revenge on a dumb animal!" cried Starbuck. "An animal that attacked you only because of its blind instinct! Madness! To be angry with a dumb thing, Captain Ahab, seems like blasphemy — an insult against God."

"Listen to me, Starbuck," said Ahab, more quietly. "All the things that we can see are only masks made of cardboard. But in every event — in every living act — there is something unknown but reasonable behind the mask. If a man wants to strike, he must strike through the mask! How can a prisoner reach the outside except by breaking through the wall? To me, the white whale is that wall. Sometimes I think there is nothing beyond it. But that is enough. He provokes me. He hurts me. I see in him great strength, and great evil behind it. That evil thing is what I hate most of all. Whether the white whale is the agent or the master, I will hit that hate at him. Don't talk to me of blasphemy, man. I'd strike the sun if it insulted me."
Starbuck said nothing. He turned pale and looked down.
"The crew, man, the crew!" said Ahab. "Aren't they all with me against the white whale? Look at them! Stand up among them, Starbuck. Look — they are all with me. Only you are left."
Starbuck said quietly to himself, "God keep me! Keep us all!" But he did not speak against Ahab again.

The steward brought a big jug full of strong drink. Ahab told the three mates to stand in front of him with their lances, and the three harpooners with their harpoons. He made the mates cross their lances in front of him, and he put his hand on the point where they met. As he touched them, he looked into the eyes of each of the mates, as if he wanted to put his own fiery will into them. Stubb and Flask looked away. Starbuck looked down.
Then he told the harpooners to take the iron heads off their harpoons and turn them upside down, so that the hollow metal sockets could be used as cups. He filled them with the fiery drink.
"Drink, you harpooners!" he cried. "Drink and swear, you men who will stand in the front of the deadly whaleboat — death to Moby Dick! God hunt us all, if we do not hunt Moby Dick to his death!"

The harpooners raised the cups and drank. "Death to Moby Dick!" they shouted, and all the crew shouted with them. Starbuck turned pale and trembled. Then Ahab went back into his cabin, and the men slowly went back to their work.
Sunset
That evening, Ahab sat alone in his cabin, looking out of the window at the sea behind the ship. The sun was going down, and the water was red and gold.
"I leave a white and troubled wake," he said to himself. "Wherever I sail, the water turns pale behind me. Envious waves rise up to cover my track, but I do not care.

"The sun is going down. It is setting in the sea, as it does every evening. And it goes down so peacefully! But I — I cannot enjoy any beautiful thing. I have the power to understand beauty, but not the power to feel it. Damned in the middle of paradise! Good night, good night.
"It was easy to make the men follow me. They were like a heap of gunpowder, and I was the match. Only Starbuck was difficult. But even he will follow me now, because he is too weak to fight me.

"They think I am mad. Starbuck thinks so. But I am more than mad. I am madness made mad! I know exactly what I am doing. My fixed purpose runs on iron rails, and nothing can stop it. Over the deep valleys, through the hearts of mountains, under the rivers — I rush straight ahead! Nothing stands in my way."
Dusk
At the same time, Starbuck was standing by the main mast, thinking.

"My soul is defeated," he said to himself. "I am defeated by a madman! He told the crew his plan, and I could do nothing. I saw his purpose in his eyes, and I felt that I must help him, though I hate it. He will drive us all to death, and I must go with him. What a terrible old man! He wants no one above him, but he rules everyone below him like a king!

"Oh, I see my bad end. But I will help him. I must. I cannot fight him, because he is the captain, and because his will is stronger than mine. But oh, God! I wish I could. I think of my wife and my child, far away in Nantucket. Will I ever see them again? Oh, life! I feel the danger now. I am like a man in a dark forest, and wild animals are all around me. Help me, God, to stay strong!"
From the front of the ship came the sound of the sailors singing and laughing.
The First Night Watch
Stubb was alone on deck, smoking his pipe and thinking.

"Ha! ha! ha! ha! hem! Clear my throat! I've been thinking about it ever since, and the result is: ha, ha! Why? Because a laugh is the wisest, easiest answer to all that's strange. Whatever happens, there's always one comfort — everything is fixed by fate. I heard everything that the old man said to Starbuck. Starbuck felt the same as I did the other night, when the old man spoke to me. Well, I'll laugh. Life is a joke. Whatever comes, I'll go to it laughing."
Midnight
Down in the front of the ship, in the forecastle, the sailors had a party. They had drunk the captain's drink, and they were happy and excited. They sang and danced.

A sailor from Nantucket sang a song about whaling. A sailor from the Isle of Man said that the gold coin would bring bad luck. A Dutch sailor slept and woke up and slept again. A French sailor wanted to dance, and he called for Pip and his tambourine. Pip played, and men from Holland, Iceland, Malta, Sicily, the Azores, China and Tahiti all danced together. Some danced so wildly that they nearly broke their legs.
A young Tahitian sailor lay on a mat and dreamed of the green hills and the dark-eyed girls of his island. An old sailor from the Isle of Man looked at the sky and said that a storm was coming.

Then a Spanish sailor began to make jokes about Daggoo's black skin. Daggoo became angry and jumped up, ready to fight. "Who's afraid of black?" he cried. In a moment, all the sailors were standing in a circle around them, shouting, "A ring! A ring!"

But just then, the storm came. Lightning flashed across the sky, and thunder roared. "Hands by the halyards! In topgallant sails!" shouted the mate. The fight was forgotten, and everyone ran to take in the sails before the wind could tear them. Only little Pip was left behind. He crawled under the windlass, frightened, with his tambourine in his hands.

"Oh, thunder! Oh, lightning!" he cried. "Jimmini, what a squall! Oh, I wish I was home in Alabama. White squalls, white whales! I heard them talking. The old man made them swear to hunt the white whale. Oh, big white God up there somewhere in the darkness, have mercy on this small black boy down here! Save him from all the men who have no hearts to be afraid!"

I, Ishmael, was one of that crew. My shouts went up with the rest, and I swore with them. Because of the fear in my soul, I shouted louder than the others. A wild, mysterious feeling was in me, and Ahab's terrible hatred seemed to be mine too. I listened eagerly to everything about that murderous monster, against whom I and all the others had sworn revenge.

For some time, sailors had told stories about a white whale that swam alone in the seas where sperm whales are hunted. Not all whalemen had heard of him. Only a few had seen him. And very few of those had fought him and lived to tell the story.

The stories about him were strange and frightening. Some sailors said that Moby Dick was everywhere at once — that he had been seen in different oceans at the same time. Others said that he could never die. Harpoons had been thrown into him many times, and he always swam away. Some said that, after a fight, they had seen him swimming quietly again, without a wound, as if nothing had happened.

But the most frightening thing about him was not his size or his colour. It was his intelligence. Many times, he had seemed to run away from the boats in terror. Then, suddenly, he turned and attacked them, breaking the boats into small pieces and sending the men back to their ship, or to the bottom of the sea. Some whalemen believed that he did this on purpose, with cruel, evil intelligence.

Moby Dick had a strange snow-white forehead with deep wrinkles, and a high white hump on his back. The rest of his body was spotted and streaked with white, like marble. His lower jaw was crooked, like a sickle. Old harpoons were stuck in his sides.
How Ahab Lost His Leg

On his last voyage, Ahab's boats had attacked Moby Dick. Three boats were broken around him, and the men and oars were thrown into the water. Then Ahab took a long knife, stood up in his broken boat, and tried to reach the whale's heart with it, like an angry man trying to kill an elephant with a small knife. At that moment, the whale suddenly swept its crooked jaw under the boat and cut off Ahab's leg, as a farmer cuts a blade of grass.

After that, Ahab had felt a wild desire for revenge. The pain in his body and the pain in his soul became one. On the long voyage home, he lay in his bed for many months, and he went mad. Sometimes he was so wild that his men had to tie him up in his hammock. His crazy shouting filled the ship.

But when the ship sailed into calmer seas, his madness seemed to go away. He came up on deck and gave his orders calmly. His officers thanked God that he was better. In reality, his madness had not gone. It had only gone deeper inside him, where nobody could see it. His great intelligence was still there, but now it served his mad purpose. He did not lose his reason; he used his reason to plan his madness.

In his mind, the white whale had become the symbol of all the evil in the world — all the things that torture men, that hurt them and confuse them, and that drive them mad. All the pain of all the ages seemed to be there, in Moby Dick. He wanted to fight all of that, and kill it, by killing the whale.

When the Pequod was ready to sail again, Ahab hid his mad plan from Peleg and Bildad, and from everybody else in Nantucket. If they had known, they would never have given him the ship. But he did not hide it from his crew. And we, the crew, were with him.

Why did we follow him? I cannot fully explain it. Perhaps it was his strong will. Perhaps it was the gold. Perhaps some evil power made us all mad together. I only know that the white whale swam in our minds as he swam in the sea. For Ahab, he was the enemy. For us, he was a terrible, unknown god.
The Whiteness of the Whale
What frightened me most about Moby Dick was something that is hard to explain: his whiteness.

White is usually a beautiful colour. It is the colour of purity and goodness. Brides wear white. Kings have often worn white robes. In many religions, white is the colour of God and the angels. So why is the whiteness of the whale so frightening?

Because whiteness also has another side. Think of the great white bear of the North Pole, or the white shark of the warm seas. Their whiteness makes them seem even more terrible. Think of the white face of a dead man, or of a ghost dressed in a white sheet. Think of the endless white snow of the mountains, or of a white sea in a fog. There is a strange, silent emptiness in whiteness.

Perhaps it is because white is not really a colour at all. It is the absence of colour — and at the same time, it is all colours mixed together. When we look at a white landscape, we feel the empty, cold universe, without meaning and without God. All the beautiful colours of nature are only like paint on the outside of things. Underneath, there is nothing but white emptiness.
And that is why the white whale was so terrible to me. In his whiteness, I saw the emptiness of the world. Is it any wonder, then, that the crew felt a deep fear when they thought of him?
Strange Sounds

One night, a sailor named Archy, who was passing buckets of water along a line of men, whispered to the man next to him, "Did you hear that noise? There's somebody down in the hold. I heard a cough." The other man laughed at him. But Archy was sure. "There's somebody down there that we haven't seen on deck," he said. "I think the old man knows about it. Remember the dark figures that came on board in Nantucket, before we sailed?"
The Charts

At night, Ahab often sat alone in his cabin with big old maps — charts of the oceans — spread out on the table in front of him. He studied them for hours. With a pencil, he drew lines across the empty blue spaces.

What was he doing? He was trying to find Moby Dick. Sperm whales, like birds, travel along fixed routes at different times of the year. They follow their food. Whalemen know these routes, and they know which seas are good for whaling in which season. Ahab had collected all the information he could find from the logbooks of many ships. He knew where Moby Dick had been seen, and when. And he knew that every year, in a certain season, the white whale was likely to be in a certain part of the Pacific Ocean, near the equator. That was where Ahab wanted to meet him. But it was still a year away. Until then, the Pequod would hunt whales in other seas, as on any normal voyage.

The thought of Moby Dick never left Ahab, even in his sleep. Sometimes, in the middle of the night, he woke up screaming and ran out of his cabin, as if his bed were on fire. He was tortured by his own thoughts. His mad purpose had become a living thing inside him, eating him from the inside like a vulture.
Whales That Fight Back

Some people on land may think that the story of Moby Dick is impossible — that no whale could be so clever and so dangerous. But it is true that whales sometimes fight back. I know of many cases. Some whales have been chased by different ships for years, and have become famous among whalemen, with names like Timor Tom or New Zealand Jack.

And whales have even sunk ships. In 1820, a large sperm whale attacked the whaling ship Essex in the Pacific. It hit the ship twice with its huge head, and broke a hole in her side. The ship sank. Her crew escaped in small boats and suffered terribly for many weeks before a few of them were rescued. So the story of the white whale is not impossible at all.
Ahab's Thoughts

Ahab knew that his crew would not stay excited about the white whale for ever. Sailors are simple men, he thought. They need money and they need action. If months passed without any whales, they might turn against him. Starbuck, too, might try to take the ship away from him. So Ahab decided to let the Pequod hunt whales normally until they found Moby Dick. That would keep the men busy and happy.
The Mat-Maker

It was a cloudy, quiet afternoon. Queequeg and I were weaving a mat on the deck. I passed a thread backwards and forwards between the long threads, and Queequeg pushed it down with a piece of wood. It seemed to me like the loom of Time. The fixed threads were necessity; my hand moving the thread was free will; and Queequeg's piece of wood, hitting the threads in different ways, was chance.
Suddenly, a wild cry came from above. It was Tashtego, at the mast-head.
"There she blows! There! There! There! She blows! She blows!"
"Where-away?"
"On the lee-beam, about two miles off! A school of them!"
Immediately, everyone on the ship was moving. The sperm whales were swimming along the surface, about two miles away, blowing up spouts of water into the air.
"Lower the boats!" Ahab shouted. "Clear away the boats!"

And then something happened that nobody expected. Five dark figures appeared on deck, as if they had come out of the air. They were Ahab's secret crew — the men we had heard in the hold! Four of them had yellow skin and wore black Chinese jackets. The fifth was a tall, dark man with a white turban on his head and one white tooth sticking out from his lips. His name was Fedallah. Nobody had ever seen him before. They went straight to a spare boat, which everyone had thought was only for emergencies, and they got it ready. It was Ahab's boat. He would hunt whales himself, with his own private crew.
