The sailors stared at them in amazement. But there was no time to ask questions. "Lower away, men!" cried the mates.
The Chase

We rowed fast towards the whales. I was in Starbuck's boat, with Queequeg as harpooner. Stubb, with his pipe in his mouth, encouraged his men in a calm, friendly voice. "Pull, my children! Pull, my little ones! Why don't you pull? Pull your backs out! Easy, easy! Don't be in a hurry. But pull, damn you, pull!" Flask stood on the back of his boat, jumping up and down with excitement.
Ahab's boat was the fastest. His dark men rowed like machines.
The sky grew darker, and the wind began to rise. A storm was coming. The whales went down under the water and came up again further away. Starbuck's boat was separated from the others.
"There's white water ahead!" whispered Starbuck. "Get ready, Queequeg!"

Queequeg stood up in the front of the boat with his harpoon. Just as a huge whale rose out of the water in front of us, he threw it. At the same moment, the storm hit us. The boat was thrown into the air. The whale touched it and swam away, and the harpoon slid out of its back. We were all thrown into the sea. When we came up, the boat was full of water, and the wind and the waves were all around us.
We climbed back into the half-sunk boat. The other boats were gone. The ship was gone. It was getting dark, and the storm was getting worse. We were alone in the middle of the ocean.

Starbuck lit a lantern and gave it to Queequeg, who held it up on a pole, as a sign of hope in the darkness. All night long we sat in the water-filled boat, wet and cold, waiting. Queequeg held up the lantern the whole night, like a man without hope holding up hope in the middle of despair.

At dawn, through the fog, we suddenly saw the Pequod. She was coming straight towards us! She was going to run over us! We jumped into the sea just as the great ship hit our boat. We were pulled on board, half dead, but alive.
My Will
When I was warm and dry again, I asked Stubb if this sort of thing happened often in whaling.
"Very often," he said. "It's nothing."
"And is it normal," I asked Flask, "for the mates to send their boats into a storm, in the dark, when they can't see anything?"
"Of course," said Flask. "That's whaling."

So I decided that if death was so close in this business, I should be ready for it. I went down to my bed and wrote my will. Queequeg was my witness. When I had finished, I felt calm and happy, as if a stone had rolled away from my heart. Now I could laugh at death. I had already died once, in a way; everything after this was extra life, a gift.
Fedallah

After that day, all the sailors talked about Fedallah and his men. Who were they? Where had they come from? How had Ahab hidden them on the ship? Some sailors said that Fedallah was the devil himself, and that Ahab had sold his soul to him. Stubb said it seriously and laughed at the same time.

Ahab's officers were especially surprised. A whaling captain usually does not lower his own boat. It is too dangerous for him, because the ship needs her captain. And Ahab had only one leg! Peleg and Bildad would never have allowed it. That was why he had hidden his men.
But Fedallah stayed mysterious. He hardly ever spoke. He was always near Ahab, watching him, like his shadow. At night he stood on deck looking at the sea. He seemed to be part of Ahab's dark secret.

chapters.title: Part 13 — The Spirit-Spout and the Albatross

paragraphs.t: Days and weeks passed. The Pequod sailed slowly south through the Atlantic, past the islands of the Azores, past the coast of Africa, towards the Cape of Good Hope.
The Spirit-Spout

One clear night, when the moon was full and the sea was like silver, Fedallah was standing at the main mast-head. Suddenly he cried out in a strange voice that sounded almost like a ghost's: "There she blows!"
Far away, in the moonlight, there was a silvery jet of water, rising and falling. It was a whale's spout — but a strange one. It looked like a ghost on the water.
Everyone on the ship ran to look. Ahab ordered the men to put up every sail, and the Pequod rushed through the night towards the spout. But the spout was not seen again that night.

A few nights later, the same silvery spout appeared again in the moonlight, far ahead of the ship. And again, it disappeared when we came closer. This happened night after night. It was always in front of us, always far away. It seemed to be calling us, leading us on.
The sailors began to whisper that it was a spirit — or that it was Moby Dick himself, leading us further and further into wild and dangerous seas, so that he could turn and destroy us there.

After the Cape of Good Hope, the sea became wild and stormy. The ship rolled and pitched in the enormous waves. Black sea birds flew around us, screaming. Every morning they sat on the ropes, as if they thought our ship was an empty, abandoned wreck. Through all those terrible days, Ahab stood on the deck in the wind and rain. When the storm was very strong, he tied himself to the ship with ropes, so that the waves would not wash him away. He hardly spoke, and he never smiled. He only looked out over the stormy sea, with his eyes full of his terrible purpose.
The Albatross
South-east of the Cape, the Pequod met another ship — a whaling ship called the Albatross. She was on her way home, after more than four years at sea.

She looked like a ghost. Her sides were white, bleached by the sun and the salt water, like the bones of a dead walrus. Long, grey seaweed hung from her. At her mast-heads stood men with long beards, dressed in skins. They looked at us without moving, like old prophets. They did not seem to see us at all.
As the two ships came close, Ahab shouted with his trumpet, "Ship ahoy! Have you seen the White Whale?"
The other captain raised his trumpet to answer, but at that moment it fell from his hand into the sea. He tried to shout without it, but the wind took his voice away. We could not hear his answer.
At the same moment, a strange thing happened. Small fish that had been swimming peacefully next to the Pequod for many days suddenly turned and swam away to the Albatross.
"Swim away from me, do you?" said Ahab sadly, looking at the water. The ships passed each other and sailed away in opposite directions.

Then Ahab shouted to the other ship: "This is the Pequod, going round the world! Tell them at home to send all future letters to the Pacific Ocean! And if I do not come home in three years, tell them to send letters to—" But the other ship was already too far away to hear.

"Round the world!" I thought. "We sail round and round the world, but where are we going? To find the same troubles we left behind? To chase a dream that runs away from us, or a phantom that leads us to our death?"
Meetings at Sea

The Pequod did not stop to talk with the Albatross, and this surprised me. Usually, when two whaling ships meet at sea, they stop and the crews visit each other. This visit is called a gam. The captains go on board one ship, and the mates go on board the other. They exchange news from home, letters, and information about where the whales are. It is a happy, friendly custom. Far from land, in the empty ocean, whalemen are like brothers.
But Ahab did not want news from home. He only wanted news of the white whale. And since the Albatross could not tell him about Moby Dick, he did not want to stop.

Not long after the Albatross, we met another whaling ship, the Town-Ho. This time there was a gam, and the crew of the Town-Ho gave us news of the white whale. They also told a strange and terrible story. Ahab never heard it, but our sailors did. Later, I told the story to some Spanish friends in Lima, in a hotel called the Golden Inn. This is how I told it.

"Gentlemen," I said, "some years ago, the Town-Ho was sailing in the Pacific Ocean, near the equator. One day, the sailors discovered that the ship was leaking. Water was coming in through a hole somewhere below. They had to work at the pumps every day to keep the ship from sinking. The captain decided to sail to the nearest port to repair her.

"On board the Town-Ho there was a sailor called Steelkilt. He came from the Great Lakes, in the north of America. He was a tall, strong, proud man, and the other sailors admired him. Everyone liked him, except one man: the mate, Radney.
"Radney was an ugly, rough man from Martha's Vineyard. He was jealous of Steelkilt, because Steelkilt was handsome and popular. Radney hated him and wanted to humiliate him.

"One evening, after Steelkilt had worked very hard at the pumps, Radney ordered him to take a broom and sweep the deck, and then to clean up the dirt left by the pigs that ran loose on board. This was a job for a boy, not for a strong sailor, and everyone knew that Radney wanted to insult him.
"Steelkilt refused politely. 'That is not my job,' he said. 'There are boys on the ship for that.'
"Radney was furious. He took a heavy hammer and came close to Steelkilt, raising it over his head. 'Do it!' he shouted.

"Steelkilt stepped back slowly, and Radney followed him. Steelkilt warned him: 'If you touch me with that hammer, I'll kill you.' But Radney did not listen. He touched Steelkilt's cheek with the hammer. At once, Steelkilt hit him in the face, and broke his jaw. Radney fell to the deck, bleeding like a whale.

"Then there was a mutiny. Steelkilt and some of his friends fought against the officers and locked themselves in the front of the ship. The captain came with a gun and told them to come out and go back to work. They refused unless the captain promised not to punish Steelkilt. The captain did not promise. So he locked them in below, without food or water.

"After some days, hungry and thirsty, most of the men gave up and came out. In the end, only Steelkilt and two others were left. Then the two others betrayed Steelkilt. They tied him up and handed him over to the captain. The captain tied all three of them to the ropes and whipped the two traitors. But when he was going to whip Steelkilt, Steelkilt whispered something to him, and the captain stepped back, frightened. He did not touch him.
"Then Radney, with his broken jaw, came up and took the whip. He whipped Steelkilt himself, very hard, while Steelkilt said nothing.

"When he was free, Steelkilt decided to kill Radney. He made a secret plan. Every night, Radney had to stand on watch alone. Steelkilt would wait until he was asleep, and then he would kill him with a heavy iron ball tied in a bag.
"But, gentlemen, before he could do it, God did it for him.

"The very next day, at dawn, the man at the mast-head shouted that he had seen a whale. It was a huge white whale — Moby Dick! The boats were lowered, and Radney, in the front of his boat, threw his harpoon into the whale. At that moment, the whale rose up under the boat, and Radney was thrown into the sea, right in front of the whale's head. The great white whale opened his crooked jaw, took Radney in his teeth, and went down with him into the deep. Radney was never seen again.

"When the Town-Ho reached land at last, Steelkilt and most of the crew ran away. The captain had to find new sailors to take the ship home. I have heard that Steelkilt is still alive somewhere, and that he still sails."
When I finished, my Spanish friends asked me if the story was really true.
"Gentlemen," I said, "I swear it on the Bible. I have met men who sailed on the Town-Ho. I have spoken to Steelkilt's friends. It is all true."

chapters.title: Part 15 — Pictures of Whales and the Giant Squid

paragraphs.t: Bad Pictures

If you want to know what a whale really looks like, do not trust the pictures in books. Most of them are completely wrong. Old painters drew whales like monsters from fairy tales, with heads like dragons, or bodies like huge fish with scales. Even in modern scientific books, the pictures are often bad. Why? Because the artists have never seen a living whale. A whale on a beach, dead and broken, does not look like a whale in the sea. And a living whale shows only a small part of its body above the water. So the only way to know what a whale looks like is to go whaling yourself. But that is dangerous. You may be broken to pieces by the whale before you have a chance to look at him properly.
There are a few good pictures, though, made by French artists, which show whaling scenes with real energy and truth: the boats, the harpooners, the great whale rising out of the sea.
Whales in Bone, Wood and Stars

Sailors on whaling ships also make their own pictures. In their free time, they carve whales and whaling scenes on whale teeth and bones, using only their knives. This art is called scrimshaw. Some of it is very fine and delicate.

And if you look carefully, you can see the shape of whales everywhere: in the clouds, in the mountains, even in the stars at night. There are groups of stars in the sky that look like a whale. I have seen them, sitting at the mast-head, on beautiful clear nights.
Brit

As we sailed north-east from the island of Crozet, we came into a part of the ocean where the water looked like a yellow field of wheat. This yellow stuff is called brit. It is made of millions of tiny sea creatures. Right whales feed on it. They swim slowly through the yellow water with their mouths open, and the brit stays in their long, thin whalebone, like a sieve.
We saw many right whales feeding there, swimming slowly, like mowers cutting grass in a field. But we did not hunt them, because the Pequod hunted only sperm whales.

Looking at the sea, I thought how terrible and how beautiful it is. On land, everything is familiar and safe. But the sea is cruel. Its creatures eat each other, and have done so since the world began. And yet, in the middle of all that danger, there is a green, peaceful island in every man's soul. Do not leave it, or you may never come back.
The Giant Squid

One quiet, sunny morning, Daggoo, at the main mast-head, saw something strange in the sea, far away. It was a great white shape, rising slowly from the deep, shining like snow. Then it sank again. Then it rose once more.
"There! There again!" cried Daggoo. "The White Whale, the White Whale!"
Immediately the boats were lowered. Ahab stood in the front of his boat, and all the men rowed hard towards the white shape. But when we came close, it was not Moby Dick.

It was the strangest thing a man could see in the sea: an enormous, soft, white mass, long and wide, floating on the water. From its centre came a great number of long arms, curling and twisting like snakes, as if they wanted to catch anything near them. It had no face. It looked like nothing living. It was a giant squid.
As we watched, it slowly sank again and disappeared.
"I would rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him," said Starbuck, very pale, "than have seen that white ghost!"
Ahab said nothing. He turned his boat and went back to the ship.

Very few whalemen have ever seen the giant squid, and those who see it usually go home and talk about it for the rest of their lives. Some believe it is the largest living creature in the ocean. But Queequeg had a different idea. "When you see him squid," he said, "then you quick see him sperm whale." Sperm whales eat squid, he explained, so where there are squid, there are sperm whales.
The Line

Before I describe our first whale, I must tell you about the whale-line — the long rope tied to the harpoon. It is about two hundred fathoms long — more than a thousand feet. It lies in a wooden tub in the middle of the whaleboat, coiled round and round very carefully, so that it can run out fast without getting tangled. From the tub it goes all round the boat, over the men's heads and hands, between their legs, to the front, where it is tied to the harpoon.

When the harpoon hits the whale and the whale dives, the line runs out with terrible speed. It flies through the boat like a snake. If it catches a man's arm or leg, it can pull him into the sea, or cut him in half. So, when the line is running, the men sit very still, and they look as calm as if they were in a church. But they are sitting in the middle of a hundred dangers. All men live surrounded by whale-lines, in a way. All are born with ropes around their necks. But only when they are caught in the sudden turn of death do they understand the silent dangers of life.
The First Whale

After the giant squid, the weather became calm and sunny. One day I was at the mast-head again, half asleep, dreaming, when suddenly I saw it: a huge sperm whale, lying quietly on the surface of the sea, not far away, spouting gently like a man smoking a pipe on a warm afternoon.
"There she blows!" I shouted.
In a moment, the boats were in the water. The whale heard us and went down, but soon he came up again, closer. Stubb's boat was the nearest.

"Start her, start her, my men!" said Stubb, with his pipe in his mouth. "Don't hurry yourselves. Take plenty of time — but start her. Start her like thunder-claps, that's all. Start her, Tashtego! Start her, my boy!"
His men rowed fast, and Tashtego stood up with his harpoon.
"Stand up, Tashtego! Give it to him!"

The harpoon flew. The whale felt it and rushed forward, pulling the boat behind him through the water. The line went hissing out of the tub, so fast that smoke rose from the wood where it rubbed. The boat flew over the waves. Water came in over the sides. The men held tight.

When the whale began to tire, Stubb's men pulled on the line, bringing the boat close to his side. Then Stubb took his long, sharp lance and pushed it again and again into the whale's body, turning it, looking for his life. At last the whale's spout became red. He was spouting blood. His life was coming out of him.
He rolled and struggled in the red water. Then a terrible shiver went through his great body, and he turned over on his side, dead.
"He's dead, Mr Stubb," said Daggoo.
"Yes," said Stubb, taking his pipe out of his mouth and shaking out the ashes. For a moment he stood looking at the huge dead body. Then he lit his pipe again.
The Harpooner's Work

I must say something about the harpooner's job. In a whaleboat, the harpooner rows like everyone else until the very last moment. He has to row as hard as he can, until he is completely out of breath. Then, suddenly, he has to stand up and throw his heavy harpoon with all his strength and perfect aim. It is not surprising that so many harpoons miss. A tired man cannot throw well. If the harpooner could rest before throwing, many more whales would be caught.
Stubb's Supper
We tied the dead whale to the side of the ship with heavy chains. It was night now, and the work of cutting it up would begin in the morning.
Stubb was very happy. He wanted to eat a steak from the whale's tail. He told Daggoo to cut one for him, and he called the old black cook, Fleece, to cook it.

Fleece was a very old man, with bad knees. He came slowly, complaining. Stubb ate his steak by the light of a lantern, while thousands of sharks swam around the dead whale in the dark water below, tearing pieces of meat from its body with their teeth. You could hear them biting and fighting.
"Cook," said Stubb, "this steak is too tough. And those sharks are making too much noise. Go and preach to them. Tell them to be quiet and to eat politely."

So the poor old cook leaned over the side of the ship with his lantern and spoke to the sharks. "Fellow-creatures," he said, "I'm told to tell you to stop that damned noise. You hear? Stop that damned smacking of your lips! Your nature is to be sharks, I know. But you must control your nature. A shark that controls himself is an angel. And remember — no matter how much you eat, you must share with your neighbours."
"Well done, old Fleece!" laughed Stubb. "That's Christianity! Go on!"

"No use going on," said Fleece. "The damned sharks will never listen. They don't hear anything. They're just stuffing their stomachs, and when their stomachs are full, they won't hear anything at all. They'll go to sleep." He raised his lantern and gave them his blessing: "Cursed fellow-creatures! Make all the noise you want. Fill your stomachs until they burst — and then die!"

Then Stubb complained about the steak again and told Fleece how to cook whale meat properly in the future. The old man went back to his bed, grumbling. "Wish, by gor, whale eat him, instead of him eat whale," he said. "He's more of a shark than Massa Shark himself."
Whale Meat

Is whale meat good to eat? Some people in the past thought so. In old France and England, kings and rich people ate whale meat at their feasts. But today, few people want to eat it. It is too rich and too oily. Sailors sometimes eat the brains of small whales, which they say taste like calf's brains. But most people are disgusted by the idea of eating such a huge creature, perhaps because it seems too much like eating a man.

And yet, do we not eat cows and pigs? Do we not kill animals every day for our food and our clothes? The man who eats beef with a knife and fork, then complains about whalemen who eat a whale, should look at himself first.

chapters.title: Part 17 — Sharks, the Head and the Jeroboam

paragraphs.t: The Sharks

That night, there were so many sharks around the dead whale that the mates feared they would eat it all before the morning. So Queequeg and another sailor stood on a platform over the side of the ship, with lanterns, and killed the sharks with long, sharp spades, cutting into their heads. But the more sharks they killed, the more came. The sharks were so mad with hunger that they attacked each other. They bit their own wounds and ate their own insides.

When Queequeg pulled a dead shark onto the deck to take its skin, its jaws suddenly closed and almost cut off his hand. The shark was dead, but its body was still alive with hate. "Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said my friend, shaking his hand in pain. "Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be a very bad god."
Cutting In

The next morning, the work began. This is called cutting in. The mates stood on a platform over the side of the ship, with long, sharp spades. They cut a hole in the whale's body, near the head, and pushed a huge iron hook into it. The hook was tied to a heavy rope that went up to the top of the mast.

Then the sailors pulled on the rope, singing, and the hook began to lift a long strip of the whale's thick skin and fat. As the strip went up, the whale turned round and round in the water, and the fat came off in a spiral, like the peel of an orange. This long, thick strip is called the blanket piece. It went up into the air and then down into a dark room below the deck, where men cut it into smaller pieces.

The whale's fat, or blubber, is about a foot thick. It keeps the whale warm in the coldest seas, like a thick coat. In the same way, a man should keep his own warmth inside him, whatever the weather outside. Be cool at the equator, warm at the poles, like the whale!
The Funeral

When all the blubber was off, the sailors cut the whale's head off, and let the white, naked body go. It floated away slowly, and birds and sharks came to eat it. It was like a funeral: the screaming birds were the mourners.

And even after its death, the whale frightened ships. Ships that saw the white body floating far away, with the birds over it, often thought that it was a rock or a dangerous reef. They wrote it on their charts, and for years afterwards, other ships sailed carefully around that empty place in the sea. That is how men's beliefs often work: they continue long after the truth has gone.
The Head

The great head of the whale hung over the side of the ship, held by chains. At noon, when the men had gone to eat, Ahab came and stood alone in front of it. He looked at it for a long time. Then he spoke.

"Speak, you great and ancient head," he said, "hanging there, without a beard. Tell us the secret thing that is in you. Of all divers, you have dived the deepest. You have seen the bottom of the sea, where sailors lie forgotten, and where ships have gone down. You have seen murdered men thrown into the sea, and ships sink with all their crews. Oh, head! You have seen enough to break the planets. And yet you are silent!"
"Sail ho!" cried a voice from the mast-head. Another ship was coming.
"Ah, that is good," said Ahab, standing up straight. "That lively cry would wake a dead man."
The Jeroboam

The ship was the Jeroboam, from Nantucket. She came close, and her captain, Mayhew, rowed over in a boat. But he did not come on board, because there was a terrible disease on his ship, and he did not want to give it to us. So he stood in his boat and talked from there.

In the boat with him was a strange young man with freckles and long yellow hair. He was wearing a long coat, and he looked like a religious fanatic. This was Gabriel. Stubb whispered to me that he had heard about him from other ships. He had been a member of a strange religious group in America. On board the Jeroboam, he had declared that he was the archangel Gabriel, and most of the sailors believed him and were afraid of him. He had so much power over them that the captain could not even punish him.
Ahab asked Captain Mayhew if he had seen Moby Dick.

Yes, they had. Some time ago, the Jeroboam had met the white whale. Gabriel had warned the crew not to attack him. "The white whale is the Shaker God," he said. But the mate, Macey, did not listen. He lowered his boat and went after the whale. As he stood up in the front of the boat to throw his lance, the whale rose up suddenly and hit him with its tail. Macey was thrown high into the air and fell into the sea, fifty yards away. He was dead. Nobody else in the boat was hurt.
"Do you intend to hunt the white whale?" Captain Mayhew asked Ahab.
"Yes," said Ahab.
"Think, think of the blasphemer!" cried Gabriel, pointing at Ahab. "Dead, and down there! Beware of the blasphemer's end!"

Ahab turned away. Then he remembered that there was a letter on the Pequod for someone on the Jeroboam. Ships often carry letters for other ships, hoping to meet them at sea. He found it, old and dirty. It was for Mr Macey, the dead mate — from his wife.

Ahab put the letter on the end of a long pole and held it out to the boat. But Gabriel took a knife, stuck it through the letter, and threw it back. It fell at Ahab's feet. "Nay, keep it thyself," cried Gabriel. "Thou art soon going that way!"
Then the boat rowed back to the Jeroboam, and Gabriel's wild laughter came back to us over the water.

chapters.title: Part 18 — The Monkey-Rope and Two Heads

paragraphs.t: The Monkey-Rope

During the cutting in, someone had to go down onto the whale's body in the water, to put the great hook into the blubber. This was the harpooner's job. Queequeg was Starbuck's harpooner, so he had to do it. He stood on the slippery back of the dead whale, half in the water, with sharks all around him.

To keep him safe, he was tied to a long rope, and I was tied to the other end of it on the ship. This rope is called the monkey-rope. My job was to hold it and pull him up if he fell or if the sharks came too close. But the rope was tied round both our bodies. So if Queequeg fell into the sea and sank, I would be pulled in after him, and we would both drown.

I understood then that I was not completely free. My life depended on another man's. If he made a mistake, I would die for it. I was like his Siamese twin. And then I thought: every man in the world is in the same situation. We are all tied to other people by invisible monkey-ropes. If your banker fails, you lose your money. If the doctor makes a mistake, you die. We all depend on each other.

Poor Queequeg worked hard, jumping over the whale's back, hitting the sharks away with his spade, while the waves washed over him. When he came back on board, wet and tired, the steward brought him a cup of ginger and water to drink, instead of the brandy he wanted. Stubb was angry. "Ginger! Do you think a cannibal can be warmed up with ginger? Give him a glass of grog!"
Two Whales

A few days later, we saw a right whale. Ahab gave orders to kill it, which surprised the sailors, because the Pequod usually hunted only sperm whales. Stubb and Flask killed it and brought it to the ship.
"Why does the old man want this ugly right whale?" Flask asked Stubb, as they rowed back.
"Didn't you hear?" said Stubb. "Fedallah told him that a ship with a sperm whale's head on one side and a right whale's head on the other can never be turned over by a storm."
"Do you think that's true?"
"I don't know. But I don't like that Fedallah. Have you noticed that he always hides his tail? I think he keeps it coiled up in his pocket. He's the devil, Flask, I tell you. The devil in disguise."
"Why does Ahab keep him on board, then?"
"I think the old man has made a deal with him. He has sold his soul to him, in exchange for Moby Dick. If I meet that devil one night, I'll pull out his tail, and see what happens."

So now the Pequod had two whale heads hanging from her sides: a sperm whale's head on one side, and a right whale's head on the other. With the heavy weight on both sides, she was balanced again. I thought of the philosophers: if you put the head of one philosopher on one side of your mind and the head of another philosopher on the other side, your mind will be balanced too — but heavy!

Meanwhile, I noticed that Fedallah stood looking at the right whale's head, and then at his own hand, as if comparing the lines in them. And when Ahab and Fedallah stood together on the deck, it seemed as if Fedallah's shadow was mixed with Ahab's, and became longer.
The Two Heads Compared
Now, while the two heads were hanging there, let us compare them.

The sperm whale's head is noble and grand. It is a huge, smooth, square block, like a great wall. It has a dignity, like an old king. On each side, low down, there is a small eye — much too small for such a huge animal. Because the eyes are on the sides of his head, the sperm whale sees two different pictures at the same time, one on each side, and cannot see straight in front. How can his brain understand two things at once? Perhaps this explains why sperm whales sometimes seem confused when they are attacked by several boats. Its ear is even smaller — a hole so small that you could hardly put a pen in it. And yet a whale hears better than any animal. The lesson is: do not judge things by their size.

The right whale's head is very different. It is ugly and strange, like a giant shoe. Its huge lips look like they could close around a whole boat. Inside its mouth hangs the long, black whalebone, like hair, through which it eats the brit. Its tongue alone gives a great deal of oil. Compared to the sperm whale, the right whale looks like a stupid, ugly animal, while the sperm whale looks like a thinker. The sperm whale is a philosopher, I think, and the right whale is just a hungry stomach.
The Front of the Head

The front of a sperm whale's head is like a huge wall, completely without bones. It is made of a very tough, elastic material, like the hardest leather. Behind it, there is a great mass of oil and fat. This makes the whole head work like a giant battering-ram. A sperm whale can hit a ship with its head and break a hole in it, as the whale did to the Essex. And the whale feels no pain, because there is nothing there to break.
The Tun

Inside the top of the head, there is a big empty space, a kind of natural tank, which whalemen call the case, or the tun, like a huge barrel. It is full of the best and purest oil — the spermaceti. In a big whale, the case can hold about five hundred gallons. When the whale is alive, the spermaceti is liquid and clear. When it meets the cold air, it becomes white and solid, like wax. It makes the finest candles in the world.
Tashtego Falls In

To get the spermaceti out, a man must climb onto the top of the whale's head, make a hole in the case, and lower a bucket into it, like a man getting water from a well. Then the full bucket is pulled up, emptied, and lowered again.

Tashtego did this job for our sperm whale's head, which was still hanging over the side of the ship. He went up, made a hole, and began to bring up bucket after bucket of the precious oil, while the men below emptied them. After a long time, the case was almost empty, and Tashtego had to push the bucket deeper and deeper inside.
Suddenly — I don't know how it happened — Tashtego slipped and fell head first into the hole! The thick oil closed over him, and he disappeared inside the whale's head.

"Man overboard!" cried Daggoo, who was the first to see it. He climbed up onto the head to help. But at that moment, there was a terrible noise. One of the great hooks that held the head had broken. The huge head swung for a moment, then fell into the sea and began to sink — with Tashtego inside it!
Everyone screamed. Daggoo jumped back onto the ship just in time. The head went down slowly into the deep water, carrying poor Tashtego with it, like a coffin.
But before anyone could do anything, a naked figure jumped from the side of the ship into the sea, with a sword in his hand. It was Queequeg! He dived down after the head and disappeared.
The men watched the water in silence. A minute passed. Another minute. Nothing. "He's lost too," someone whispered.

Then, suddenly, an arm came out of the water, and then a head — Queequeg's head! And with his other arm he was pulling a second man by his long black hair. It was Tashtego! Queequeg had dived down to the sinking head, cut a hole in its side with his sword, put his arm inside and pulled Tashtego out, head first, like a midwife bringing a baby into the world.

They were pulled on board. Tashtego was half dead, but he soon recovered. Queequeg was a hero again. And I thought: what a strange death that would have been — to drown in the sweetest, most precious oil in the world!
The Whale's Face

A sperm whale has no real face. It has no nose. Its eyes and ears are on the sides of its head, far away from each other. When you look at the front of its head, you see only a great empty wall, with deep wrinkles across it, like a mountain landscape or a wide prairie. And yet this face has a great dignity. It looks like the face of a god. It seems to say: "I am beyond your understanding." The more I study it, the less I understand it. How can I explain the whale's face, when I cannot even explain the face of a man?
The Brain

A sperm whale's head is enormous, but its brain is very small — not bigger than a man's. It is hidden deep inside the head, behind the case, like a nut inside a thick shell. You could go twenty feet into the head without finding it. But perhaps the whale's real strength is not in its brain, but in its long spine. A strong spine makes a strong character. And the sperm whale has the strongest spine in the world. I wish more men had a spine like that.

chapters.title: Part 20 — The Virgin and More About Whales

paragraphs.t: The Virgin

One day we met a German whaling ship called the Jungfrau, which means "the Virgin". Her captain, Derick De Deer, rowed over to us in his boat. He was holding something in his hand. When he came closer, we saw that it was an oil can.
"Look at him!" laughed Stubb. "He's coming to beg for oil!"

It was true. The German ship had not caught a single whale on its voyage. It had no oil left, not even for its lamps. The captain asked politely if we could give him some. Starbuck filled his can, and the German was very grateful.

But just as he was going back to his ship, the men at the mast-heads of both ships shouted at the same time: "Whales!" A group of eight whales was swimming not far away. Captain De Deer forgot his oil can and rowed back to his ship as fast as he could. Then the boats of both ships were lowered, and there was a race.

The Germans were ahead at first. But our men rowed harder and harder. Among the whales was a big, old one, who swam slowly and strangely, because one of his fins was missing. He was blowing a weak, short spout. "Who's got some paregoric?" laughed Stubb. "He has a stomach ache!"

The three boats of the Pequod — Starbuck's, Stubb's and Flask's — passed the German boat. All three harpooners threw their harpoons into the old whale at the same moment. The whale dived deep, pulling all three boats after him. Then he came up again, tired and slow. The mates killed him with their lances. The poor old whale had been blind and sick, and he died sadly.

When the men began to cut into his body, they found something strange: the point of an old stone harpoon, deep in his flesh, completely covered by new skin. It must have been there for many years — maybe since before America was discovered! Someone had hunted this whale long, long ago, and he had survived.
But then the whale began to sink. He was so heavy that he pulled the ship down to one side, and we had to cut the chains to let him go. He sank to the bottom of the sea, and all our work was lost.

Meanwhile, the German ship had seen another spout, and its boats were chasing it. But it was a fin-back whale, which is too fast to catch. We watched them row after it for a long time, getting further and further away, with no hope of success.
The Honour of Whaling

Whaling is one of the oldest and most noble professions in the world. The first whaleman, I believe, was Perseus, the Greek hero, who killed a sea monster to save the beautiful Andromeda. Saint George, who killed the dragon, was probably also a whaleman: the "dragon" was really a whale. Hercules was swallowed by a whale, like Jonah, and came out alive. Even the Indian god Vishnu, the old books say, once took the form of a whale. So whalemen belong to a great family of heroes and gods.
Jonah

Some people say that the story of Jonah cannot be true. How could a man live inside a whale for three days? An old sailor once told me that perhaps Jonah was not inside the whale at all, but inside a ship called The Whale. Others say that Jonah hid in the dead body of a whale. But I believe the Bible.
The Javelin

Sometimes, when a whale swims too fast for the boats to come close, the mate throws his lance from far away, like a javelin. This is called pitchpoling. Stubb was the best at it. He threw his long lance high into the air, and it came down like a bird into the whale's back. Then he pulled it back with the rope tied to it, and threw it again, and again, until the whale was dead.
The Spout

What comes out of a whale's head when it spouts? Many people think it is water. But I believe that it is only breath — warm, wet air, like the steam from a kettle. Nobody knows for sure, because nobody has been close enough to touch it without danger. Some sailors say that if the spout touches your skin, it burns. Some say that if it gets into your eyes, it makes you blind.

When I see the great white spout rising from the whale's head, I think it is like the misty thoughts of a deep thinker. I believe that a whale is always thinking. It seems to me that the mist over his head is like the cloud that rises from the head of a philosopher, deep in thought. And sometimes, in the spout, there is a rainbow, which only shines on such clouds of thought — as if heaven itself were blessing his mind.
The Tail

The tail of the sperm whale is the most beautiful and powerful thing in nature. It is about twenty feet wide, flat and smooth. It can move in five different ways: to swim forward, to fight, to sweep the water around it, to slap the surface, and to rise high into the air as the whale dives down. With one hit of his tail, a whale can throw a boat and all its men high into the air. And yet, he can also use it very gently, to touch the water like a hand. In his tail, the whale has both great power and great grace. The more I think about it, the less I understand it. If I cannot even understand his tail, how can I understand his head? And how can I understand the whole whale?

The Pequod sailed east across the Indian Ocean towards Java and the islands of Asia. To reach the Pacific, we had to go through the Straits of Sunda, a narrow passage between the islands of Sumatra and Java. Many ships go through it, and it is a famous place for pirates.

As we came near the Straits, we saw an amazing sight. Ahead of us, spread across the sea in a huge half-circle, there were hundreds — no, thousands — of sperm whales, all swimming together. Their spouts rose into the air like the chimneys of a great city. It was like an army, a Grand Armada.
Sperm whales sometimes travel in huge groups like this, when they are afraid. Too many ships hunt them now, and they gather together for protection.

Ahab ordered every sail to be raised, and we chased the great herd. But just then, Tashtego shouted from the mast-head that there were other ships behind us — small, fast Malay pirate boats. They were coming after us! So now we were chasing the whales, and the pirates were chasing us. "Ahab," I thought, "is hunting the whale, and death is hunting Ahab."

But the Pequod was faster than the pirates, and soon they were left behind. Then the whales seemed to become confused. They stopped running and began to swim round and round in circles. The boats were lowered.
In the Centre

Queequeg threw his harpoon into a whale, and the whale pulled our boat at great speed right into the middle of the herd. Whales were all around us, crashing through the water. We expected to be killed at any moment. Then the harpoon came out of the whale, and we found ourselves in a strange place.

In the centre of the herd, the water was completely calm, like a quiet lake. Hundreds of whales were swimming slowly around us, peaceful and unafraid. They were the females and the young ones, the mothers and their babies, kept safe in the middle of the herd by the others swimming in circles around them.

The young whales came close to our boat and looked at us with curious eyes, like puppies. Queequeg touched their heads, and Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, and they did not move away. Some of them seemed to sniff at us, like dogs.

And under the water, in that clear sea, we saw something even more wonderful. Deep down, the mother whales were feeding their babies with milk. We could see the babies, small and new, still tied to their mothers by a long cord, the way human babies are tied to their mothers when they are born. One of the babies looked up at us as it drank, as if we were only a piece of floating seaweed.

It was the most peaceful thing I have ever seen. And I thought: in the same way, although the storms of life are all around me, deep in the centre of my soul there is a calm place where I can rest, and where I am always happy.
The Panic

But our peace did not last. In the outer circles of the herd, some of the other boats had attacked whales. One whale had been wounded with a cutting-spade, which was still tied to the end of a rope. The whale swam wildly through the herd, dragging the spade behind him. The sharp spade cut and hurt the other whales as it passed them, and they became mad with fear.

Suddenly, the calm circle broke. The whales began to rush in all directions. The great herd moved towards us, and we were in the middle of a storm of whales. We rowed for our lives, pushing between the huge bodies. They almost crushed our boat. At last we escaped, and the whales swam away, faster than ever, until they disappeared over the horizon.
After all that excitement, we had caught only one whale. Many whales had been wounded, but they had escaped. Whaling is like that. There is always more danger than profit.
Whale Families

Sperm whales live in two kinds of groups. Some groups are made of females with their young ones, led by one big, strong male, like a sultan with his wives. He is very jealous. If another male comes near, there is a terrible fight. But when he grows old, he leaves the group and lives alone, grumpy and wise. The other kind of group is made of young males, who are wild and quarrelsome, like students. When they are hunted, they do not help each other. Each one runs away alone.
Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish

Whalemen have a simple law about who owns a whale. If a whale is tied by a rope to a boat or a ship, it is a Fast-Fish, and it belongs to the people who are holding the rope. If it is not tied to anything, it is a Loose-Fish, and anyone can take it. This law is very simple, but it can explain the whole world. What is a slave but a Fast-Fish? What is America, in 1492, but a Loose-Fish, taken by Columbus for Spain? And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish too?
The Rose-bud

A few weeks later, we noticed a terrible smell coming over the sea. Soon we saw a French whaling ship, the Rose-bud. Tied to her sides were two dead whales — very old and rotten. One of them had died of disease, and the other had been found dead in the sea. They gave almost no oil, and they smelled horrible.

"Ah," said Stubb, holding his nose. "A rose-bud! What a sweet smell!" He looked at the rotten whales with a clever look in his eyes. "I think there might be something valuable in one of them," he said quietly. "These French don't know anything about whaling."

He rowed over to the French ship. The captain did not speak English, but the mate, who came from the island of Guernsey, did. The mate hated his captain and wanted to get rid of the stinking whales. So Stubb and the mate made a plan. Stubb told the mate to tell his captain that the rotten whales were very dangerous, and that they could give the whole crew a terrible fever.

The mate translated, but not exactly what Stubb said. He told the captain that the American gentleman had warned them about the danger of disease. The French captain was very frightened. He thanked Stubb, ordered his men to cut the whales loose at once, and sailed away.

As soon as the French ship had gone, Stubb rowed to the sick whale, which was now a Loose-Fish, and began to dig into its body with a spade. The smell was terrible. The men thought he was mad. But after some time, a sweet, strong perfume came up from the rotten whale. Stubb shouted with joy. He pulled out handfuls of a soft, grey substance like wax. It was ambergris — one of the most valuable things in the world!
He had taken six handfuls when Ahab called the boat back to the ship. Stubb would have taken more, but he had to obey.
Ambergris

Ambergris is found inside the bodies of sick sperm whales. It is used to make the finest perfumes, and it costs more than gold. Isn't it strange that the most beautiful perfume comes from the stomach of a sick, rotten whale? It is like the Bible, which says that the bodies of the dead will rise again in glory. Out of the worst things, sometimes the best things come.
Pip
Now I must tell you the sad story of little Pip.
Pip had always stayed on the ship when the boats were lowered, because he was only a boy. But one day, one of the men in Stubb's boat hurt his hand, and Pip had to take his place.

The first time, Pip was very frightened. When Tashtego's harpoon hit a whale and the whale hit the boat with its tail, Pip jumped out of the boat in terror. He got caught in the line, which was running out after the whale, and it began to choke him. Tashtego had to cut the line to save him, and they lost the whale.

Stubb was angry. "Stick to the boat, Pip," he said. "Or by the Lord, I won't pick you up if you jump again. We can't afford to lose whales for the likes of you. A whale would sell for thirty times what you would, Pip, in Alabama. Remember that, and don't jump any more."
But the next time, Pip jumped again. This time there was no line around him, and Stubb kept his promise. The boat went on after the whale and left Pip alone in the middle of the ocean.

It was a beautiful, calm day. The sea was smooth and blue, and it went on for ever in all directions. Pip floated alone, his little black head like a dark spot in the enormous sea. He watched the boats getting smaller and smaller until they disappeared. The loneliness was terrible.

Stubb had not really intended to leave him for long. He thought the other boats would pick him up. But the other boats were busy chasing whales too, and nobody saw him. At last, by chance, the Pequod itself found him and saved him.

But from that hour, Pip was never the same. He walked around the ship like an idiot. People said he was mad. The sea had kept his body alive, but it had drowned his soul. He had gone down to the bottom of the ocean in his mind, and there he had seen strange things: the wonders of the deep, the beginning of the world, the foot of God. And men call that madness. But perhaps his madness was the wisdom of heaven. What man calls madness, heaven may call wisdom.
A Squeeze of the Hand

When the spermaceti is taken from the whale's head and left in the air, it becomes hard, with small lumps in it. To make it smooth again, the sailors must sit around big tubs and squeeze the lumps with their hands until they become liquid.

I sat with several other sailors around a tub one sunny afternoon, squeezing spermaceti. It was the most pleasant work I ever did. The spermaceti was soft and warm, and it smelled sweet, like spring flowers. My hands became soft, and my heart became soft too. All the anger and bad feelings I had ever felt disappeared.

I squeezed and squeezed, until I found myself squeezing the hands of the other sailors by mistake, thinking they were lumps of spermaceti. And I felt such love for them! I looked into their eyes, and I wanted to say: "Oh, my dear fellow men, why should we ever be angry with each other? Let us all squeeze hands, and squeeze ourselves into each other, and become one in the milk of kindness."

I have learned that happiness is not found in great ideas or big dreams. It is found in simple things: your wife, your heart, your bed, your table, the saddle, the fireside, the country. If I could, I would squeeze spermaceti for ever.
The Try-Works

On the deck of a whaling ship, between the masts, there is a strange structure made of bricks, like a small factory. These are the try-works — two huge ovens with two big iron pots on top, where the blubber is boiled to make oil.

When a whale has been cut in, the fat is cut into small pieces, and the pieces are thrown into the pots. The fire is made with the dry, crispy pieces of fat that are left after boiling — so the whale burns its own body to make its own oil. The smoke is black and smells terrible, like a funeral pyre.

At night, the try-works are a wild sight. The fires burn red in the darkness. The harpooners stand around them, with their faces lit by the flames, stirring the boiling oil with long forks, telling terrible stories and laughing. Their faces look like devils'. The ship rushes through the black night with her red fire burning, like a ship from hell.

One night, I was at the helm, steering the ship, while the try-works were burning. I looked into the fire for a long time, and I became sleepy. I closed my eyes for a moment. When I opened them, I was confused. I could not see the compass. Everything around me was black, except the red fire. I felt that the ship was running backwards, away from her direction. Then I understood: I had turned round in my sleep, and I was facing the back of the ship! I was holding the helm the wrong way, and the ship was turning dangerously against the wind. In another moment she would have turned over! I quickly turned round and corrected her course.

From that night I learned a lesson: do not look too long into the fire. Do not let artificial light deceive you. Tomorrow the natural sun will show you the truth. The sun hides neither the sea nor the dark side of the earth, which is two thirds of it. A man who sees only joy is a fool, but a man who sees only sadness is also lost. There is a wisdom that is sadness, and there is a sadness that is madness. Be careful not to let it take you.
The Lamp

On a whaling ship, there is always light. On merchant ships, the sailors sleep in the dark, because oil is expensive. But on a whaling ship, there is so much oil that the sailors can burn lamps all night. The whaleman lives in light, like a king.
Clearing Up

When the oil is boiled and cooled, it is poured into big barrels, called casks, and stored deep down in the ship. Then the whole ship is cleaned. The sailors wash the decks with soap and water, and scrub everything until it shines. The ship looks as clean as a new house. The men put on fresh clothes, and they look like brides.

But they have hardly finished when the cry comes again from the mast-head: "There she blows!" And the boats are lowered again, and the whole bloody, dirty, smoky work begins once more. Such is the life of a whaleman. Every time we finish, we must start again.

chapters.title: Part 24 — The Doubloon and the Samuel Enderby

paragraphs.t: The Doubloon
The gold coin that Ahab had nailed to the main mast was still there, shining in the sun. Nobody touched it. It belonged to the man who would first see Moby Dick.

It was a Spanish coin from Ecuador, a country on the equator, on the west coast of South America. On it there were pictures of three mountains. On the first mountain there was a flame; on the second, a tower; on the third, a rooster crowing. Above them was part of the zodiac — the circle of the stars — with the sun entering the sign of Libra, the scales.
One morning Ahab stood in front of the coin and looked at it for a long time.

"There's something important in all things," he said, "or the world would mean nothing. Look at these mountains. They are proud, like Lucifer. The tower — that is Ahab. The volcano — that is Ahab. The brave, unafraid, victorious rooster — that is Ahab too. All are Ahab. This round gold is like the round world, which, like a magician's glass, shows each man only his own face."

When he went away, Starbuck came and looked at the coin. "I see three mountains," he said, "like the Trinity. And there is darkness in the valleys between them. But the sun of righteousness shines above them. Oh, Father, keep me from losing my faith!" And he went away quickly, afraid of his own thoughts.

Then Stubb came. He studied the zodiac and laughed. "Here is the story of a man's life, from spring to winter," he said, "and it ends in the fish sign. There's a sermon in these stars. Jolly, he's never sad! Ha, ha!"
Then Flask came, and he only said: "I see nothing here but a round thing made of gold. Sixteen dollars. At two cents a cigar, that's nine hundred and sixty cigars." And he went away.

The old Manxman came, and said that the white whale would be seen in the month of the sign on the coin. Queequeg came, and compared the signs with the tattoos on his body. Fedallah came, and bowed to the coin, because he worshipped fire and the sun.

Last of all, little Pip came, and he looked at the coin and said, "I look, you look, he looks; we look, you look, they look." He said this again and again. Then he said, "Here's the ship's navel. Here's her navel. And they're all burning to unscrew it. But unscrew your navel, and what happens? Your bottom falls off!" Poor mad Pip. Sometimes the mad say wise things.
The Samuel Enderby
Some weeks later, we met an English whaling ship, the Samuel Enderby, from London. Ahab shouted, "Have you seen the White Whale?"
The English captain held up his arm. It was not a real arm. It was made of white whalebone, like Ahab's leg. "Do you see this?" he cried.

Ahab was so excited that he ordered his boat to be lowered at once, and he was rowed over to the English ship. But he could not climb up the side with his ivory leg. The English captain understood, and he lowered a big hook from the ship. Ahab sat on it, and they pulled him up like a whale.
The English captain, whose name was Boomer, was a big, happy, friendly man. "Shake hands, sir," he said. "Bone to bone — an ivory arm and an ivory leg! Ha, ha!"
"Where did you see him?" asked Ahab. "How long ago?"

Captain Boomer told his story. He had seen Moby Dick on the equator, the season before. He did not know at first that it was the famous white whale. He saw a group of whales and lowered his boats. Then suddenly a huge white whale rose out of the water, with a milky white head and hump, and many old harpoons in his side. One of the harpoons caught the line, and the whale broke Boomer's boat in half with his tail. Captain Boomer tried to hold on to the harpoon, but the whale went down, and the harpoon cut his arm badly. The arm became infected, and the ship's doctor, Dr Bunger, had to cut it off.
"Did you ever meet him again?" asked Ahab.

"Twice," said Boomer. "But I didn't go after him. One arm is enough for me. He's welcome to the arm he has, since I can't help it. But he won't have the other. No more white whales for me. I lowered for him once, and that's enough. There would be great glory in killing him, I know; and there's a ship-load of precious oil in him. But he's best left alone. Don't you think so, Captain?"
"He is. But he will still be hunted, for all that," said Ahab. "Which way was he going?"
"Bless my soul!" said Boomer. "East, I think. Is your captain crazy?" he whispered to Fedallah.

But Ahab was already climbing down into his boat. "Back to the ship!" he shouted to his men. He was in such a hurry that, as he jumped into the boat, he hit his ivory leg against the side, and it was badly cracked.
Measuring a Whale

I have studied whales in many ways. I once saw the skeleton of a great sperm whale on an island in the South Pacific, in a beautiful green temple made of trees. The islanders worshipped it like a god. I measured it with a rope, and I had the measurements tattooed on my right arm, because I had no paper to write on. The skeleton was seventy-two feet long. A living whale of that size would be about ninety feet long.
Will the Whales Disappear?

Some people worry that so many whales are being killed that one day there will be none left, like the buffalo on the American prairies, which are being killed in their thousands. I do not think so. The whales are clever. They have learned to live in groups for protection, and to go to the coldest seas of the North and South Poles, where no ship can follow them. The whale existed before men, and I believe he will exist after them. The oceans are too large, and the whale is too strong. He will survive.
When Ahab got back to the Pequod, his ivory leg was badly damaged. It looked strong enough, but he did not trust it. He had a secret reason for this.

Before the Pequod left Nantucket, Ahab had been found one night lying on the ground, unconscious. His ivory leg had broken, and the sharp end had hurt him badly in the body, near the groin. It was a terrible wound, and it took a long time to heal. That was why he had stayed hidden in his house before the voyage, and why he did not come on deck during the first days at sea. He did not want anyone to know. The wound seemed to him like another attack by the white whale — as if all his pains were connected, one leading to the next, like a family. Every sadness has a father and a grandfather. Even the gods, he thought, must have their sorrows.
Now, after the meeting with the Samuel Enderby, he called the ship's carpenter and ordered him to make a new leg at once.
The Carpenter

The carpenter of the Pequod was an old man who could do everything. He could repair a boat, make a chair, pull a tooth, cut hair, and build a coffin. He worked with his hands, without thinking. He was not stupid, but he never asked questions. He did every job in the same calm way, whether he was making a toy for a sailor or a leg for the captain. He was like a pocket knife with many blades: useful for everything, but without a soul. He talked to himself as he worked, but only because talking helped his hands to work.

He set up his bench on the deck, next to the try-works. The blacksmith, an old man called Perth, started his fire to make the iron parts. The carpenter found a good piece of whalebone, the jaw of a sperm whale, and began to cut and file it into the shape of a leg. White dust flew around him.
Ahab and the Carpenter
Late at night, Ahab came to see how the work was going. He stood beside the carpenter and watched him for some time.
"Well, carpenter," he said. "How goes the leg?"
"Well, sir. I'm just measuring it."
"Good. You make legs, and you also make coffins, don't you? Tell me, carpenter, if you could make a whole man, how would you make him?"
The carpenter did not understand, but Ahab answered his own question.

"I would order a complete man," he said, "made to my design. First, fifty feet high. Then, a chest made like a tunnel, with arms three feet thick. No heart at all. A forehead of brass, and about a quarter of an acre of fine brains. And let me see — shall I order eyes to see outwards? No, but put a skylight on top of his head, to light up the inside. There, take the order, and away."
The carpenter thought that the captain was making a joke, and laughed politely. But Ahab was not joking.

"Carpenter," he said after a while, "I'll pay you for this leg. But tell me something. Even though my real leg is gone, I can still feel it. Here, where your new leg will be, I can feel my old leg, as if it were still there. Isn't that strange? And if I can feel a leg that is not there, carpenter, how do you know that there isn't some invisible thing standing right here, where you stand? Some spirit, some ghost, that is here although you cannot see it?"
The carpenter looked around nervously.

"Oh, Life!" said Ahab. "Here I am, proud as a Greek god, and yet I owe my leg to this foolish carpenter. I hate being dependent on anyone. I wish I could be as free as air. But I am in debt to the whole world. How long will it be before I am paid back?" He turned and went away.

The carpenter shook his head and went on working. "He's a strange one, the old man," he said to himself. "Very strange. I've heard that Stubb calls him queer. Queer, queer — that's the only word for him. Well, I'll make his leg, and then I'll make his coffin, if he wants one. A man must be ready for anything."

chapters.title: Part 26 — Starbuck, Ahab and Queequeg's Coffin

paragraphs.t: The Leak
One morning, the sailors noticed that oil was coming up with the water from the bottom of the ship. Some of the casks in the hold must be leaking. Starbuck went down to Ahab's cabin to tell him.
Ahab was studying his charts. He did not look up.
"Captain," said Starbuck, "the oil in the hold is leaking. We must bring up the casks and repair them. It will take a day or two."
"Bring them up? Now, when we are getting close to Japan? Stop for a week to repair a few old barrels?"
"Either we do that, sir, or we lose more oil in one day than we can make in a year. What we came twenty thousand miles to get is worth saving, sir."
"So it is, so it is — if we get it."
"I was speaking of the oil in the hold, sir."
"And I was not speaking of it. Go! Let it leak! I'm all leaks myself. I'm leaking in a leaky ship. But I don't stop to repair myself. I go on. Go, Starbuck. Back to the deck!"
"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, his face red. "What will the owners say?"

"Let the owners stand on Nantucket beach and shout louder than the storms. What do I care? The owners, Starbuck! You are always talking about those mean owners, as if they were my conscience. But listen — the only real owner of anything is its commander. And my conscience is in this ship's keel. Up to the deck!"
"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, coming further into the cabin, "a better man than I might forgive you. But I ask you, please —"
Ahab took a loaded musket from the wall and pointed it at Starbuck.
"There is one God who is Lord over the earth," he cried, "and one Captain who is lord over the Pequod. On deck!"

For a moment, Starbuck's eyes burned. Then he spoke very calmly. "You have insulted me, sir. But I will not ask you to beware of Starbuck. You would only laugh. But let Ahab beware of Ahab. Beware of yourself, old man."

He went out. Ahab stood still, with the musket in his hand. Then he said to himself, "He's brave, but he obeys. What did he say? Ahab, beware of Ahab? There's something in that." After a while, he went up on deck and said to Starbuck, "You are too good a man, Starbuck." And he gave the order to repair the casks.
Queequeg's Fever

To find the leaking casks, the men had to go deep down into the dark, wet bottom of the hold, and move the heavy barrels one by one. Queequeg worked there for many days. It was cold and damp, and the air was bad. And then my poor friend caught a terrible fever.

He lay in his hammock for days, getting thinner and weaker. His eyes became bigger and rounder, and they seemed to look into a far-away distance. Everybody thought that he would die. He thought so too.

Then he called me and told me something strange. On his island, he said, when a man died, his body was put in a canoe and sent out to sea, to float away to the stars. Queequeg did not want to be thrown into the sea in his hammock, like a dead sailor, to be eaten by sharks. He wanted a canoe — a coffin shaped like his island canoes.

So the carpenter made him a coffin out of dark wood. When it was ready, Queequeg asked to see it. He lay down in it to try it, with his harpoon beside him and his little idol Yojo on his chest. He asked for some biscuit and a bottle of fresh water to be put in it with him, for his journey. Then he said, "It is good," and they lifted him out and put him back in his hammock.

Little Pip came and looked at him. He took Queequeg's hand. "Poor rover! Will you never finish your weary roving? Where are you going now? If you go to the Antilles, where the waves wash the beaches of white lilies, will you do a small thing for me? Find a boy called Pip, who has been missing for a long time. I think he is in those far Antilles. If you find him, comfort him, because he must be very sad. Look! He left his tambourine behind. I found it. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Now, Queequeg, die, and I'll beat your dead march."
Queequeg Decides to Live

But then, to everyone's surprise, Queequeg began to get better. In a few days, he was well again. When we asked him how, he said that he had suddenly remembered something important that he had to do on land, and so he had decided not to die. "If a man decides to live," he said, "a small sickness cannot kill him. Only a whale or a storm can kill a man who has decided to live."

He used the coffin as a sea chest, to keep his clothes in. And in his free time, he carved designs on the lid — copies of the tattoos on his body. A wise man on his island had made those tattoos long ago. They told the whole story of heaven and earth, and a way to find the truth. But Queequeg could not read them. So his body was a living book of mysteries that even he could not understand — and one day, those mysteries would die with him.
Ahab looked at Queequeg one morning, as he sat carving the lid, and said, "Oh, devilish torture! Here is a book that its owner cannot read."

chapters.title: Part 27 — The Harpoon and the Bachelor

paragraphs.t: The Pacific

At last we sailed into the great Pacific Ocean. For me, it was the answer to a hundred prayers I had made as a boy. This calm, wide ocean, which covers half the world, seems to hold the spirits of all the dead who lie in it. Its soft waves seem to whisper secrets. It rolls gently between the countries of Asia and the shores of America, and its islands are like the small, green dreams of a sleeping giant.

But Ahab did not feel any of this peace. To him, the Pacific was only the ocean where Moby Dick lived. Every day he looked at the sea, and every night he looked at his charts. We were getting closer to the place where he had decided to fight.
The Blacksmith

The blacksmith, Perth, was an old man with burned hands and a sad face. He had not always been a sailor. Once he had been a good blacksmith on land, with a house, a wife and three children. But he began to drink, and drink destroyed everything. He lost his business. His wife and children died, one after another. At last, alone and old, he decided to die too. But the sea called him. "Come to us," the sea seemed to say. "We have a new life for you, without the pain of death." So he became a whaleman, and now he worked at his little fire on the deck of the Pequod, without complaining, and without hope.
The Forge
One night, Ahab came to the blacksmith with a bag. "Perth," he said, "I want a harpoon made — a harpoon that a thousand pairs of devils' hands could not break."

He opened the bag. Inside were many small, bent pieces of steel. "These are the nail-stubs from the shoes of racehorses," Ahab said. "They are the toughest steel in the world. Make me a harpoon of them."

Perth heated the nails in his fire and began to hammer them together. Ahab watched. When the long iron head was ready, Ahab gave him his own razors. "And here are my razors," he said, "the best steel there is. Make the barbs of my harpoon from them. I will never shave again."
When the harpoon was nearly ready, it had to be dipped into liquid to harden the steel. "Water?" asked Perth.
"No, no," said Ahab. "Not water. I want it to be hardened with something better. Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo! Come here, you pagans! Will you give me as much blood as will cover this barb?"

The three harpooners nodded. Ahab cut their arms, and the steel was hardened in their blood. As it hissed and steamed, Ahab cried out in Latin, in a terrible voice: "I do not baptize you in the name of the Father, but in the name of the devil!"

Then he fixed the iron head onto a long pole of wood, and tied a new rope to it. He held the harpoon in the air and looked at it with a wild, fierce joy. Then he went to his cabin. Behind him, Pip laughed sadly.
A Calm Sea
Near the coast of Japan, the weather was beautiful, and the sea was calm and golden. The days seemed to last for ever. Even Ahab seemed to become a little gentler.

"Oh, grassy meadows! Oh, endless spring in the soul!" he said, standing on the deck. "I wish I could rest here. But no. Life is not a single, straight path, from child to man. It goes round and round in circles. First we are babies, then boys, then men full of doubts, then believers, then unbelievers, then again babies. Where is the final harbour, where we can rest? Where is the father of the lost child? Our souls are like orphans whose mothers died when they were born. We search for our fathers, and we never find them."
Starbuck, looking at the same calm sea, said: "Lovely sea, it makes me forget the terrible things under the surface. Let faith keep away the facts. Let fancy keep away memory."
And Stubb said: "I am Stubb, and Stubb has his history. But here Stubb swears that he has always been happy!"
The Bachelor

Soon afterwards we met a ship from Nantucket called the Bachelor. She was the happiest ship I ever saw. Her voyage had been a great success. She was full to the top with oil — every cask, every room, even the captain's cabin was full of barrels. She was going home.

On her deck, there was a party. The sailors were dancing with girls from the Polynesian islands. Her captain stood proudly on the quarter-deck, waving at us. A drum was beating, and the men were singing.
"Come on board, come on board!" shouted the happy captain. "Come and share our party!"
"Have you seen the White Whale?" Ahab shouted back.
"No! Only heard of him. But I don't believe in him at all," said the captain cheerfully. "Come on board!"
"You are too happy," said Ahab. "Sail on. Have you lost any men?"
"Not enough to talk about — two islanders, that's all. But come on board, old man, come along! I'll soon take that black from your face. We're full, and we're going home!"
"You are a full ship and going home, you say. Well, then, call me an empty ship, and going out. So go your way, and I'll go mine. Forward there! Set all sail, and keep her to the wind!"

And so the happy ship sailed home with a good wind behind her, while the Pequod sailed on, against the wind, towards her dark fate. As Ahab watched the Bachelor go, he took out a small bottle of sand from Nantucket and looked at it for a long time.
The Dying Whale

A day after the Bachelor, we found a group of whales, and we killed four of them. One of them was killed by Ahab's boat. It was late in the afternoon. The sun was setting over the sea in red and gold.
As the whale died, a strange thing happened. Slowly, the great head turned towards the sun, as if the dying animal wanted to look at it one last time. Then it stopped moving. Ahab watched in silence.

"He turns and turns him to the sun," Ahab said quietly. "How slowly, but how surely! He, too, worships fire. Most faithful servant of the sun! But see — no sooner dead than death turns him round, and he looks another way. Oh, dark half of the world, where you worship fire, I believe you, but I do not trust you. Here, in the sea, the waves carry the dead, and the water has no god."
The Night Watch

That night, Ahab's boat stayed beside the dead whale, far from the ship, to keep it safe until morning. Ahab sat in the back of the boat, and Fedallah sat in the front. The other men were asleep. In the darkness, the two of them talked.
"I have dreamed it again," said Ahab.
"Of the hearses?" asked Fedallah. A hearse is the carriage that carries a dead body to the grave. "Have I not said, old man, that neither hearse nor coffin can be yours?"
"And who are buried at sea, who have no hearses?"

"But I said, old man, that before you can die on this voyage, two hearses must be seen by you on the sea. The first is not made by mortal hands. And the second must be made of wood that grew in America."
"Ha, ha!" said Ahab. "A strange sight that would be, Fedallah — a hearse with its plumes floating on the ocean, with the waves as pallbearers. We won't see such a sight soon."
"Believe it or not, you cannot die till it is seen, old man."
"And what was it you said about yourself?"
"Though it comes to the last, I shall still go before you, as your pilot."

"And when you go before me — if that ever happens — then, before I can follow you, you must still appear to me, to guide me? Was it not so? Well, I believe it all, my pilot. And I have here two promises. I will kill Moby Dick and survive."
"Take another promise, old man," said Fedallah, his eyes shining like fireflies in the dark. "Only hemp can kill you."
"The gallows, you mean? A hanging rope?" laughed Ahab. "Then I am immortal, on land and on sea!" And both were silent again, while the dawn came up grey over the sea.
The Quadrant

The season-on-the-line was coming at last — the time when Moby Dick was usually seen near the equator. Every day at noon, Ahab sat on the deck with his quadrant, a navigation instrument, and measured the height of the sun to find out exactly where the ship was.
One day, after he had made his measurement, he looked at the quadrant with anger.

"You toy!" he said. "You foolish plaything of proud men! You can tell me where I am, and where the sun is. But you cannot tell me where Moby Dick is! You cannot tell me where I shall be tomorrow at noon. Science! Curse you, you useless toy! Curse all things that lead men's eyes up to the heavens, when they should be looking at the earth! I will no longer use you to guide my ship!"
And he threw the quadrant down onto the deck and broke it with his feet — with his living foot and his ivory foot.
"From now on, the compass and the log and line will guide me," he said. "I'll find my way across the sea as the old sailors did."
Fedallah, who was standing nearby, smiled, as if he knew more than Ahab. Starbuck and Stubb, at the other side of the deck, saw everything.
"I have sat before the hot coals," whispered Starbuck to himself, "and have seen them burn down to dead ashes. Old man, your life will burn down to ashes too."
"Yes," said Stubb quietly. "Smashed it, did he? Well, it doesn't matter. Whatever happens, I'll keep on laughing. Wise Stubb — that's what they call me."

chapters.title: Part 29 — The Candles and the Musket

paragraphs.t: The Typhoon
In the warm seas near Japan, the most terrible storms in the world can appear suddenly, out of a clear blue sky. These storms are called typhoons. One evening, a typhoon hit the Pequod.

The wind tore her sails to pieces. The waves were like mountains, and they broke over the deck. One of the whaleboats — Ahab's own boat — was smashed by a wave. The thunder was so loud that we could not hear each other's voices. The rain fell in sheets. It was as dark as midnight.

Then, suddenly, a strange light appeared. At the top of each mast, and at the end of every pole, a pale white fire was burning, like the flame of a tall candle. The three masts looked like three giant candles in front of an altar. Sailors call this strange light corposants, or Saint Elmo's fire. They believe it is a sign — sometimes of good luck, but more often of danger.

Everyone stopped working and stared at the white flames. Some sailors fell on their knees. Their faces looked pale and ghostly in the white light. Stubb shouted, "The corposants have mercy on us all!" Even the harpooners were afraid.

Ahab came forward. He stood under the main mast, with his foot on the back of Fedallah, who knelt in front of him. He held up his hand to the white fire on the top of the mast, and he spoke to it in a loud voice.

"Oh, you clear spirit of clear fire! I worshipped you once, on these seas, as a Persian worshipper of fire, until you burned me, and I still have the scar. Now I know you better, and I know that the right way to worship you is to defy you! You are a great power, but you have no love and no pity. I am a man, and I have a personality, and a will of my own. You can kill me, but you cannot make me obey you. Oh, you clear spirit, of your fire you made me, and like a true child of fire, I breathe it back to you!"
At that moment, the harpoon that Ahab had forged with the blood of the harpooners — which was lying in his broken boat — began to burn with a white flame too, like a giant tongue of fire.

Starbuck took Ahab by the arm. "God, God is against you, old man! Stop! It is a bad sign. Let me take the ship home, as she should go. We have had a bad voyage, and it is going to be worse. Let us go home, while we can still save the ship and our lives!"
The sailors heard Starbuck and began to shout. They ran to the ropes, ready to turn the ship and run before the wind towards home. But Ahab grabbed the burning harpoon and held it up like a torch.

"All your oaths to hunt the White Whale are as binding as mine!" he cried. "And heart, soul and body — Ahab is bound. Look! This is how I blow out the last fear!" With one breath, he blew out the flame on the harpoon.
The sailors ran away from him in terror. Nobody spoke against him again.
Later That Night
Later, while the storm was still blowing, Stubb and Flask stood together in the darkness.
"Did you hear what Starbuck said?" asked Flask. "That God is against us?"

"Of course God is against us," said Stubb. "But that doesn't mean we will die. The ship is safe enough. Ahab put his lightning rod over the side, so the lightning will go into the sea. Don't worry, Flask. A storm is a storm."

High up on the mast, Tashtego was tying the sail. "Um, um, um," he sang to himself. "Stop that thunder! Plenty too much thunder up here. What's the use of thunder? Um, um, um. We don't want thunder; we want rum."
The Musket

At about midnight, the typhoon became weaker. Then the wind changed direction. It was now a good wind, blowing from behind, pushing the Pequod towards the place where Ahab wanted to go. Starbuck went down to the captain's cabin to tell him.
