Ahab was asleep in his cabin. As Starbuck stood in front of the door, he saw the row of loaded muskets on the wall. One of them was the same musket that Ahab had pointed at him a few weeks before.
Starbuck took it down. A terrible idea came into his head.

"He would have killed me once," he thought. "He is going to kill us all. He is leading the whole crew to death. And he won't listen to anyone. Is there no other way? Could I lock him up and take the ship home? No — he is too strong. Even with chains, he would be more dangerous than a tiger in a cage. I could not bear his howls. The only way is to kill him. If I shoot him now, while he sleeps, the ship will be saved, and the crew too. And I will see my wife and my child again. Oh, Mary! Mary! Boy! Boy! Boy! But if I do not do it, old man, who knows where you will take us? Great God, where are You? Shall I? Shall I?"
He raised the musket and pointed it at the door. His hand was shaking. At that moment, Ahab cried out in his sleep, on the other side of the door:
"Stern all! Oh, Moby Dick, I hold your heart at last!"
Starbuck stood still, as if he had been struck. Then, with a shaking hand, he put the musket back on the wall.
He went back up to the deck and said to Stubb: "He's too sound asleep, Mr Stubb. Go down and wake him, and tell him about the wind. I must watch the deck. You know what to say."

chapters.title: Part 30 — The Needle, the Line and the Rachel

paragraphs.t: The Needle

The next morning, the sea was calm again, and the sun was shining. Ahab looked at the sun, and then at the compass, and his face became pale. The sun was behind the ship — but according to the compass, we were sailing towards it! Something was wrong.
"Starbuck!" he cried. "The lightning has turned our compasses round! They point the wrong way. We are sailing west, not east!"
It was true. The lightning in the storm had reversed the magnetism of the compass needles. Now north was south, and south was north.

The sailors were terrified. Without a compass, how could we find our way? But Ahab was not afraid. He took a steel lance, broke off its point, and asked for a hammer and a needle used for sewing sails. Then, in front of all the crew, he made a new compass. He hit the steel with the hammer many times, holding it in a special way, until it became magnetic. Then he put it into the old compass and showed it to the men. The new needle pointed in the right direction.
"Look for yourselves," he cried proudly, "if Ahab is not lord of the magnet! The sun is east, and the compass swears it!"
The sailors looked at him with fear and wonder. To them, Ahab was not a man, but a magician. Their fear of him became even greater.
The Log and Line

To measure the speed of a ship, sailors use a log and line: a piece of wood tied to a long rope with knots in it. They throw it into the sea and count how many knots go out in a certain time. The Pequod had not used her log and line for a long time, and the rope had become old and weak.
Ahab ordered it to be thrown into the sea. The old Manxman held the line. "Sir, I am afraid it is too old and rotten," he said.
"Throw it," said Ahab.
The line ran out, and then suddenly it broke. The log was lost in the sea.
"I crush the quadrant, the thunder turns the needles, and now the mad sea breaks the log-line," said Ahab. "But Ahab can fix everything. Make a new line."
Pip came running towards them, talking strangely. "Pip? Who calls Pip? Pip jumped from the whaleboat. Pip's missing. Let's see if you have fished him up here, fisherman."
"Who are you, boy?" said Ahab.
"Bell-boy, sir. Ship's crier. Ding, dong, ding! Pip! Pip! Pip! One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip. Five feet high — looks cowardly — quickest known by that!"
Ahab looked at the boy. Something in his face changed. He took Pip's hand.

"Come with me," he said gently. "Ahab's cabin shall be Pip's home from now on, while Ahab lives. You touch my deepest heart, boy. You are tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings. Come, let's go down."
"What's this? Here's velvet shark-skin," said Pip, looking at Ahab's hand. "Ah, now, if poor Pip had only felt so kind a thing as this, perhaps he had never been lost!"
The Life-Buoy

A few days later, at dawn, a sailor climbed to the mast-head to take his watch. He had only been there a few minutes when he gave a cry and fell into the sea. The men ran to the side and threw the life-buoy to him — a small, light barrel that floats, for a man in the water to hold. But the barrel had been in the sun too long, and it was dry and cracked. Water came into it, and it sank, and the man sank with it. He was the first man of the Pequod to die on the voyage, and it was a bad sign.

We needed a new life-buoy. Queequeg suggested that his coffin could be used. It was empty now, and it would float well. Starbuck did not like the idea, but there was nothing else. So the carpenter closed the coffin with wood and tar, so that no water could get in, and hung it at the back of the ship, ready to be thrown to anyone who fell into the sea.

Ahab came and watched the carpenter work. "Can it be?" he said. "Here is a coffin, the symbol of death, turned into a life-buoy, the symbol of life. Can it be that, in some spiritual sense, a coffin is, after all, only a life-preserver? I'll think about that. But no. So far gone am I in the dark side of earth, that its other side, the light side, seems only uncertain twilight to me."
The Rachel
The next day, we saw a large ship coming towards us. She was the Rachel, from Nantucket. Before she came close, her captain shouted: "Have you seen a whaleboat adrift?"
But Ahab shouted, "Have you seen the White Whale?"
"Yes, yesterday. Have you seen a whaleboat adrift?"
Ahab was so excited that he could hardly answer. The Rachel's captain, a man called Gardiner, came on board. Ahab knew him; he was from Nantucket too.
"Where was he? Not killed! Not killed!" cried Ahab. "How was it?"

Captain Gardiner told his story. The day before, late in the afternoon, three of the Rachel's boats had been chasing a group of whales. Then Moby Dick had appeared, and the fourth boat had gone after him. The boat had been pulled away by the white whale, very fast, until it disappeared. They had searched all night, but they had found nothing.
Then Gardiner came close to Ahab and spoke in a broken voice.

"My boy, my own boy was in that boat. He is only twelve years old. For God's sake, Captain Ahab, I beg you, let me charter your ship for forty-eight hours. I will pay you anything. Help me search for him. Sail with me, side by side, so that we can see more of the sea. You must do it. You will do it! You have a boy too, Captain Ahab — a child, at home in Nantucket. For your own boy's sake, help me!"
The men of the Pequod listened in silence. Stubb said quietly, "He must do it. He can't refuse."
But Ahab stood still, as cold as iron.

"Captain Gardiner," he said, "I will not do it. Even now I am losing time. Goodbye, goodbye. God bless you, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go. Mr Starbuck, look at the clock. In three minutes all strangers must leave the ship. Then set the sails and keep her to her course."
Gardiner looked at him for a moment, unable to believe it. Then, without a word, he went back to his boat.

Soon the two ships were sailing away from each other. For a long time, we could see the Rachel moving backwards and forwards across the sea, searching for her lost children. She was like Rachel in the Bible, crying for her children, who were gone.
Pip and Ahab
Ahab was going up on deck. Pip took his hand and wanted to follow him.

"No, boy, you must not follow me now," said Ahab. "The hour is coming when Ahab would not frighten you away, and yet would not have you near him. There is something in you, poor boy, that seems to cure my illness. And I do not want to be cured now. Like cures like, and for this hunt, my sickness is my most desired health. Stay here below, where they shall serve you as if you were the captain. Sit here in my own chair."
"No, no, no!" cried Pip. "You have no whole body, sir. Use poor me for your missing leg. Only tread on me, sir. I ask no more, so I remain a part of you."
"Oh, boy!" said Ahab. "You make me weak. You are the only one who can soften me. Weep so, and I will murder you! Stay here. Goodbye."
When he had gone, Pip sat in the captain's chair. "Here he goes," he said. "Pip will wait here, in the captain's chair. If anyone asks for Pip, tell them that he is here."
The Hat

Now that Moby Dick was near, Ahab wanted to be the first to see him. He did not trust anyone else. He had a basket made out of rope, and he had himself pulled up in it to the top of the main mast. And he gave the end of the rope, the one that held him up, to Starbuck. Of all the men on board, he chose to put his life in the hands of the one man who had opposed him.

He sat in his basket at the top of the mast for many hours, looking at the sea in all directions. Then a black sea-hawk came down from the sky and flew round and round his head, screaming. Suddenly it took Ahab's hat in its claws and flew away with it, far out over the sea, until it was only a small black spot. Then it dropped the hat into the water.
An old story says that when an eagle took the hat off a man's head and then put it back, it meant that he would become king. But the sea-hawk did not bring back Ahab's hat.
The Delight

The next ship we met was named, ironically, the Delight. She was a sad sight. One of her whaleboats lay on her deck, completely smashed — only its broken white ribs were left, like the bones of a horse.
"Have you seen the White Whale?" Ahab shouted.
"Look!" answered the captain, pointing to the broken boat.
"Have you killed him?"
"The harpoon is not yet made that will ever do that," said the other captain sadly.

"Not made?" Ahab took his own harpoon, the one hardened in blood, and held it up. "Look here, Nantucketer! Here in this hand I hold his death! Hardened in blood, and tempered by lightning are these barbs. And I swear to temper them three times in that hot place behind the fin, where the white whale most feels his cursed life!"

"Then God keep you, old man. See that?" The captain of the Delight pointed to a body wrapped in a hammock, lying on the deck. "I bury only one of five strong men, who were alive only yesterday. But they were dead before night. Only that one I bury. The rest were buried before they died. You sail upon their tomb."
Then the crew of the Delight threw the body into the sea. As it fell into the water, some of the drops splashed onto the Pequod's side like a cold baptism.
As we sailed away, the men of the Delight saw the coffin hanging at the back of the Pequod — the coffin that was our life-buoy.
"Ha! Look there, men!" a voice shouted from the Delight. "In vain, oh strangers, you run from our sad funeral. You only turn your back to us to show us your coffin!"
The Symphony

It was a clear, blue day. The sky and the sea were so blue that you could hardly see where one ended and the other began. The air was soft and gentle, like a woman's touch. The sea moved gently, like the strong chest of a sleeping man.

Ahab stood on the deck, looking over the side, watching his shadow in the water. The beautiful day seemed to touch even his hard heart. From under his hat, a single tear fell into the sea. The whole Pacific Ocean did not contain anything as precious as that one little drop.
Starbuck saw him and came quietly to stand beside him.

"Starbuck," said Ahab. "Oh, Starbuck! It is a soft wind, and a soft sky. On a day just like this one, I killed my first whale. I was a boy-harpooner of eighteen! That was forty years ago. Forty years of whaling! Forty years of danger and storms! In those forty years, I have not spent three years on land. When I think of the life I have lived — so lonely, so far from everyone, a captain that nobody can speak to — it is like the life of a slave. And then I married a young girl, when I was over fifty. The next day I sailed for Cape Horn. She has only one mark of my head on her pillow. A wife? No — a widow, with her husband still alive!

"Yes, I have made that poor girl a widow, Starbuck. And all the madness, the anger, the boiling blood, as I hunted the whale — more like a demon than a man! What a fool old Ahab has been! Why all this struggle? Is Ahab richer or better now? Look at me. Am I not very, very old, Starbuck? I feel weak and bent, as if I were Adam, carrying all the centuries since Paradise on my back.

"God! God! Break my heart! Come close to me, Starbuck. Let me look into a human eye. It is better than looking at the sea or the sky, better than looking at God. In your eye I see the green land and the warm home. I see my wife and my child. No, no — stay on board when I go after Moby Dick. That danger will not be yours. Not with that far-away home in your eye!"

"Oh, my captain! My captain!" said Starbuck. "Noble soul! Great old heart, after all! Why should anyone chase that hated fish? Come away with me! Let us leave these deadly waters! Let us go home! Starbuck has a wife and child too, just as you have, sir. Let me change our course now! How happily we would sail home to see old Nantucket again! I think they have blue days like this in Nantucket too."

"They have, they have. I have seen them," said Ahab softly. "On summer mornings. At this time of day — yes, the boy is waking up from his afternoon sleep now. He sits up in bed, and his mother tells him about me, his cannibal old father. She tells him that I am far away on the sea, but that I will come back one day and dance with him again."

"It is my Mary, my Mary!" said Starbuck. "She promised that every morning she would carry my boy up the hill, to see the first sign of his father's ship! Yes, yes! No more! It is decided! We sail for Nantucket! Come, my captain, let us plan our course and go! Look, look! The boy's face at the window! The boy's hand on the hill!"
But Ahab turned his eyes away. He shook, like a dead tree that drops its last apple to the ground.

"What is it?" he said. "What strange, hidden, unearthly power is it that commands me? Against all my natural love and longing, I keep pushing myself forward, ready to do what in my own heart I would not dare. Is Ahab really Ahab? Is it I, or God, or who, that lifts this arm? If the sun does not move by itself, but is sent across the sky like a servant, how can my small heart beat, or my small brain think, by itself? It is God who does it, not I. We are turned round and round in this world, like that windlass there, and Fate is the handle."
Starbuck had turned away, pale as death, and walked away in despair.
Ahab crossed the deck to look over the other side. But there, reflected in the water, he saw two eyes staring up at him. Fedallah was leaning on the same rail, looking down into the sea.

chapters.title: Part 32 — The Chase: The First and Second Days

paragraphs.t: The First Day

That night, at about midnight, Ahab suddenly stood up on the deck and smelled the air, like a dog. He said that a whale must be near. He could smell the strange smell that a living sperm whale gives out over long distances. He changed the ship's course a little and ordered the sails to be reduced.

At dawn, all the men were at the mast-heads, looking at the sea. Ahab was pulled up in his basket. The sea was smooth and quiet. Then, at the same moment, all the lookouts saw it — and Ahab saw it first.
"There she blows! There she blows! A hump like a snow-hill! It is Moby Dick!"
The cry went through the whole ship. The men ran up the ropes to see. About a mile ahead, a huge white hump was moving slowly through the blue sea, sending up a tall, white spout every few seconds.
"And did none of you see it before?" cried Ahab.
"I saw him almost at the same moment, sir, as Captain Ahab did, and I cried out," said Tashtego.

"Not the same moment. Not the same — no, the doubloon is mine. Fate saved the doubloon for me. I only. None of you could have raised the White Whale first. There she blows! Lower the boats! Mr Starbuck, remember — stay on board and keep the ship. Lower!"
Ahab's boat had been repaired. It went first, with Fedallah and his dark men rowing. Stubb's and Flask's boats followed. Starbuck stayed on the ship.

As we came close, the white whale was swimming quietly, almost peacefully. The sea around him was smooth and calm. He was more beautiful than I had ever imagined — calm and gentle and grand, with a soft, white, milky body. Seabirds flew above him. In his back, the old broken harpoons stood up like the masts of sunken ships. No god, not even Jupiter in the form of a white bull swimming with a beautiful girl on his back, ever looked so majestic.
Then, slowly, he raised his great tail into the air and went down under the water.

The boats waited. A long time passed. The birds flew in circles. Then Ahab looked down into the clear water, and he saw a small white spot, rising quickly from the depths. It grew bigger and bigger. Then he saw two long, crooked rows of white teeth. It was Moby Dick's open mouth, coming straight up from below, under Ahab's boat!

Ahab turned the boat quickly. But the whale was too fast. He came up beside the boat and took the front of it in his huge jaws, the way a cat takes a mouse. His crooked lower jaw went under the boat, and his teeth came down on the wood. Ahab grabbed the jaw with his bare hands and tried to push it away. Then the jaw closed, and the boat was bitten completely in half. Ahab fell into the sea.

The whale swam round and round the broken pieces of the boat, making waves. The men in the water held onto the floating wood. Ahab, who was too old and tired to swim well, held onto a piece of the boat and shouted, "Sail on the whale! Drive him off!"

The Pequod came forward, straight towards the whale. Moby Dick swam slowly away. The other boats came and picked up Ahab and his men. Ahab lay at the bottom of Stubb's boat, exhausted, like a man trampled by elephants. For a long time he could not speak. Then he sat up.
"The harpoon?" he said. "Is it safe?"
"Yes, sir. It wasn't thrown. Here it is."
"Put it in front of me. Any men missing?"
"One, two, three, four, five — there were five oars, sir, and here are five men."

"That's good. Help me up, man. I want to stand. There, there! I see him! There! Still going away from the wind. What a spout! Let go of me! New life is running through Ahab's bones again! Set the sail! Oars out! To the helm!"
They followed the whale all day, but he swam too fast. As the night came, Ahab gave orders to follow him through the darkness, and to call him at the first sign of the whale.

"The doubloon is mine," he said to the men, "but I will leave it on the mast. Whoever sees the whale first on the day he is killed shall have it. And if he is killed on that day, then ten times its value shall be divided among you all."
The Second Day

At dawn, the lookouts saw him again. This time, Moby Dick jumped right out of the water, like a salmon jumping up a waterfall — the whole huge body, high into the air! Then he fell back with a crash that sent the white water flying high, like a mountain of snow.
"Yes, jump for the last time in the sun, Moby Dick!" cried Ahab. "Your hour and your harpoon are near! Down, down, all of you! Lower! Mr Starbuck, stay on board!"

Ahab had another boat now, a spare one. All three boats were lowered. This time, Moby Dick did not wait for them. He turned and came straight towards the boats, with his great head forward, his jaw open, and his tail beating the sea behind him.

The three boats spread out to attack him from three sides. The harpoons flew, one after another, and three of them hit him. But the whale swam round and round among the boats, so fast that the lines from the three harpoons crossed and tangled together. Ahab cut his line to free it, but it was too late. The whale pulled the lines tighter and tighter, and the boats of Stubb and Flask were pulled together and smashed against each other, like two shells on a beach. The men fell into the water.
Then the whale went down and came up right under Ahab's boat, and threw it high into the air. It turned over and fell back upside down into the sea. Ahab and his men were thrown into the water.
The Pequod came and picked up all the men. But Ahab was hurt. His ivory leg had broken off, and only a short, sharp piece of it was left. He leaned on Starbuck's shoulder.
"Yes, Starbuck," he said. "It is sweet to lean on someone sometimes, whoever he is. I wish old Ahab had leaned on others more often."
"Captain, the leg is broken," said the carpenter. "There's only a stump left."
"Even with a broken leg, Ahab is not hurt," said Ahab. "No white whale, no man and no devil can touch the real Ahab, deep inside. Count the men!"
The men were counted. One was missing.
"The Parsee!" cried Stubb. "Fedallah! He's gone."

They searched everywhere on the ship, but Fedallah was nowhere. Then Stubb remembered that he had seen him caught in the tangled lines, when Ahab's boat turned over. The whale must have pulled him down into the sea.

"Caught in the line!" cried Ahab. "My line! Gone! Gone! What does that little word mean? It sounds like a funeral bell, and old Ahab shakes like a bell tower! Fedallah gone first!" He remembered the prophecy: Fedallah would go before him, as his pilot.

"Captain Ahab," said Starbuck, "you will never, never catch him, old man. In the name of Jesus, stop this. It is worse than the devil's madness. Two days of chasing, two boats smashed to pieces. Your own leg broken again. Your dark shadow, Fedallah, gone. All the good angels have been warning you. What more do you want? Shall we follow this murderous fish until he kills every last one of us? Shall he pull us down to the bottom of the sea, or to hell? It is a sin to hunt him any more!"

"Starbuck," said Ahab, "lately I have felt strangely close to you, since the day we both saw — you know what — in each other's eyes. But in this matter of the whale, your face must be nothing to me, like an empty hand. Ahab is for ever Ahab, man. Everything that happens here was decided long ago, and it cannot be changed. You and I practised these parts a billion years before this ocean existed. Fool! I am only Fate's officer. I am following orders. And you, who are below me, must follow mine. Stand around me, men. You see an old man with only a stump of a leg, leaning on a broken lance. That is Ahab's body. But Ahab's soul is like a centipede: it walks on a hundred legs.

"Do you believe in signs? Then laugh! Before a drowning man drowns, he comes up to the surface twice. Then he comes up once more, and sinks for ever. It is the same with Moby Dick. For two days he has come up. Tomorrow will be the third day. Yes, men, he will come up once more — but only to spout for the last time! Do you feel brave, men?"
"As fearless fire," cried Stubb.
"And as mechanical," Ahab whispered to himself. Then he went to his cabin, while the carpenter made him a new leg from the white bone of the broken boat.

chapters.title: Part 33 — The Chase: The Third Day, and the Epilogue

paragraphs.t: The Third Day
The morning of the third day was clear and fresh. Again the men went up to the mast-heads, and again Ahab sat in his basket at the top of the main mast. But for many hours nobody saw the whale.

"Have we passed him?" Ahab said. "Yes, he's following us now, and we are not following him. I've gone the wrong way." He gave orders to turn the ship round. Now we were sailing against the wind, back the way we had come.
"Against the wind he now steers for the open jaw," whispered Starbuck to himself. "May God be with us all."

While he was on the mast, Ahab looked at the sea and the sky and spoke to himself. "What a lovely day again! If the world were new, made as a summer house for the angels, the day could not be lovelier. There is a lot here to think about, if Ahab had time to think. But Ahab never thinks; he only feels, feels, feels. That's enough for any man!"
At noon, the lookouts shouted. There was the spout, not far away.
"Forehead to forehead I meet you, this third time, Moby Dick!" cried Ahab. "Down, men! Lower the boats!"
Before he got into his boat, Ahab turned to Starbuck.
"Starbuck!"
"Sir?"
"For the third time my soul's ship begins this voyage, Starbuck."
"Yes, sir. You want it so."
"Some ships sail from their ports and are never seen again, Starbuck."
"That is true, sir. Very sadly true."

"Some men die when the tide goes out; some when the sea is low; some when it is high. And I feel now like a wave at its highest point, Starbuck, just before it breaks. I am old. Shake hands with me, man."
Their hands met. Their eyes met. Starbuck's tears held them together like glue.
"Oh, my captain, my captain! Noble heart — don't go! Don't go! Look, a brave man is crying. It hurts me so much to beg you!"
"Lower away!" cried Ahab, pulling his hand away. "Stand by the crew!"

The boats were lowered, and they rowed out towards the whale. As they went, Starbuck stood at the side of the ship and watched them. And he saw that Ahab's boat was followed by sharks. They swam close to it, biting at the oars as the men rowed. They followed only Ahab's boat. "Sharks!" Starbuck said to himself. "They follow him the way vultures follow armies. Oh, my God! Why do I feel so terribly calm, when I am expecting the worst?"
The First Hearse
The whale came up suddenly in front of the boats, rising out of the sea, huge and white, with water pouring from his sides. And then the men saw something horrible.
Tied to the whale's back by the tangled lines from the day before was the body of Fedallah. His clothes were torn, and his dark, open eyes looked straight at Ahab.

Ahab dropped his harpoon. "Tricked! Tricked!" he cried, breathing hard. "Yes, Parsee! I see you again. Yes, you go before me. And this, then, is the hearse that you promised — a hearse not made by human hands." The whale was the first hearse.
But Moby Dick did not attack. He seemed to want only to escape. He began to swim away, steadily, towards the open sea.
"Oh, Ahab," cried Starbuck from the ship, "even now, on the third day, it is not too late to stop. See! Moby Dick does not look for you. It is you, you, that madly look for him!"
But Ahab did not hear. His boat followed the whale.
The Second Hearse

Then the whale turned. Perhaps he was tired of being chased. Perhaps he understood at last that the ship was the source of all his enemies. He turned round and swam straight towards the Pequod, with his great white forehead in front of him, through the foaming sea.

"The whale! The whale! Turn the ship! Turn the ship!" cried Starbuck. "Oh, sweet powers of heaven, hold me close! If Starbuck must die, let him die bravely. My God, I hold on to You. Must I die like this, facing my end?"

Stubb, too, stood on the deck. "Oh, Flask," he said, "I'd give anything for one red cherry before we die! I wish we were where cherries grow. Oh, Flask, I hope my poor mother has already received some of my pay. If not, she won't get much now, because the voyage is over."

The whale hit the ship with his great head. The Pequod shook from end to end. The men fell to the deck. A great hole was broken in her side below the water, and the sea rushed in. The whale went under the ship and came up on the other side, close to Ahab's boat.
Ahab saw the Pequod sinking.
"The ship! The hearse!" he cried. "The second hearse! And its wood could only be American!" He understood the prophecy at last.

"Oh, a lonely death after a lonely life!" he cried. "Now I feel that my greatest greatness is in my greatest sorrow. Come, all you waves of my past life, and break over me in this last great wave of my death! Towards you I go, you whale that destroys everything but is never defeated. I will fight you to the end. From the heart of hell I stab at you. For hate's sake I spit my last breath at you. Let all coffins and all hearses sink together! And since neither can be mine, let me be torn to pieces while I still chase you, tied to you, you damned whale! So — I throw the spear!"

He threw the harpoon with all his strength. It went deep into the whale. The whale rushed forward, and the line ran out at great speed. It got tangled, and Ahab bent down to free it. He freed it — but the line flew round his neck like a rope round the neck of a man being hanged, and pulled him out of the boat so fast that his men did not even see him go. He disappeared into the sea. The hemp had killed him, as Fedallah had said.
For a moment, the men in the boat stood frozen. Then they turned and looked at the ship. "The ship? Great God, where is the ship?"

The Pequod was sinking. Only the tops of her masts were still above the water. On the top of the main mast, Tashtego was still there, holding a hammer, nailing Ahab's red flag to the mast. As the ship went down, a great whirlpool formed, turning round and round. It caught the last boat and the men in it, and pulled them down into the sea. Everything — the men, the boats, the broken oars — went round and round, and disappeared.

At the very last moment, a sea-hawk flew down to the top of the mast and caught at the flag with its beak. Just then, Tashtego's hammer came down and nailed the bird's wing to the wood. And so the bird of heaven, screaming, went down with Ahab's ship, like a devil that would not go to hell without dragging a living part of heaven with it.

Now small birds flew screaming over the open hole in the water. A white wave beat against its steep sides. Then the whirlpool closed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.
Epilogue
The drama is over. Why, then, does anyone come forward to tell the story? Because one man survived.

On the third day, Fedallah's place in Ahab's boat had to be filled, and I was the one who took it. When the boat was hit and turned over, I was thrown out, and I floated in the sea at a distance, watching everything happen. When I reached the place where the ship had sunk, the whirlpool had become smaller. I was pulled slowly towards its centre, round and round, like a man on a slowly turning wheel.

When I reached the centre, the black bubble in the middle burst. And suddenly, from the depths, Queequeg's coffin shot up out of the water, like a living thing, and fell beside me. It was the life-buoy, made of Queequeg's coffin. I held onto it, and it saved my life.

For almost a whole day and a whole night, I floated on that soft and funeral-like sea, holding the coffin. The sharks swam past me without touching me, as if their mouths were locked. The wild sea-hawks flew over me with their beaks closed.
On the second day, a ship came near, and at last it picked me up. It was the Rachel. She was still sailing around, searching for her missing children. But she only found another orphan.

grammar.title: Verb to be (present)
grammar.form: I am · you/we/they are · he/she/it is. Negativa: is not (isn't), are not (aren't). Pergunta: Is he...? Are you...?
grammar.explanation: O verbo to be significa ser ou estar. É o verbo mais comum do inglês. Ele aparece sozinho, antes de adjetivos (She is tired), de substantivos (He is a captain) e de lugares (They are in the ship).

grammar.title: Present simple
grammar.form: I/you/we/they work · he/she/it works. Negativa: don't / doesn't + verbo. Pergunta: Do you...? Does he...?
grammar.explanation: Usado para hábitos, rotinas, fatos e verdades gerais: The sun rises in the east. Atenção ao -s na terceira pessoa do singular (he lives, she goes, it has). Nos livros, aparece muito em diálogos e em explicações do narrador.

grammar.title: There is / there are
grammar.form: There is + singular · There are + plural. Passado: there was / there were.
grammar.explanation: Equivale a 'há' ou 'existe' em português. Use there is para uma coisa e there are para várias: There are three boats. No passado: There was a strange light.

grammar.title: Present continuous
grammar.form: am / is / are + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para ações que estão acontecendo agora ou neste período: The ship is sinking! Também é usado para planos já combinados para o futuro: We are leaving tomorrow.

grammar.title: Imperative
grammar.form: Verbo na forma básica: Come! Look! Negativo: Don't + verbo: Don't go!
grammar.explanation: Para dar ordens, conselhos e instruções. Não há sujeito: Stand up! Lower the boats! Para ser mais educado, acrescente please.

grammar.title: Can / could (ability and permission)
grammar.form: can / could + verbo básico. Negativa: cannot (can't), could not (couldn't).
grammar.explanation: Can expressa capacidade ou permissão no presente: I can swim. Could é o passado de can (He could not move) e também uma forma educada de pedir (Could you help me?).

grammar.title: Verb to be (past)
grammar.form: I/he/she/it was · you/we/they were. Negativa: wasn't / weren't.
grammar.explanation: O passado de to be: was e were. The night was cold. They were afraid. É uma das formas mais frequentes em narrativas.

grammar.title: Past simple (regular verbs)
grammar.form: verbo + -ed: walk → walked, arrive → arrived, stop → stopped. Negativa e pergunta: did not (didn't) / Did...? + verbo básico.
grammar.explanation: Para ações terminadas no passado. É o tempo principal das histórias: He opened the door and looked inside. Os verbos regulares formam o passado com -ed.

grammar.title: Past simple (irregular verbs)
grammar.form: formas próprias: go → went, see → saw, take → took, come → came, say → said...
grammar.explanation: Muitos verbos comuns não usam -ed no passado e precisam ser memorizados. Ler muito é a melhor forma de fixá-los: The whale rose out of the water. She saw him in the church.

grammar.title: Past continuous
grammar.form: was / were + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que estava em andamento no passado, muitas vezes interrompida por outra: I was writing when the Count came in. Também descreve o cenário de uma cena: The wind was blowing and the waves were rising.

grammar.title: Going to (future)
grammar.form: am / is / are going to + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para intenções e planos (I am going to meet a nobleman) e para previsões baseadas no que vemos (The ship is going to sink!). No passado, was going to indica um plano que talvez não aconteceu.

grammar.title: Will (future)
grammar.form: will ('ll) + verbo básico. Negativa: will not (won't).
grammar.explanation: Para decisões no momento da fala, promessas e previsões: I will come back. He won't escape. Em textos antigos aparece também shall, com sentido parecido (I shall wait).

grammar.title: Comparatives and superlatives
grammar.form: Curtos: -er / the -est (big, bigger, the biggest). Longos: more / the most (more beautiful, the most beautiful). Irregulares: good, better, the best; bad, worse, the worst.
grammar.explanation: Para comparar duas coisas (The sperm whale is bigger than the right whale) ou destacar uma entre todas (the largest animal in the world).

grammar.title: Present perfect
grammar.form: have / has + particípio passado (seen, done, written, arrived)
grammar.explanation: Liga o passado ao presente: experiências de vida (I have never seen such a whale), ações recentes com resultado agora (He has lost his leg) e situações que começaram no passado e continuam (I have lived here for fifty years). Não se usa com tempo passado definido (yesterday, in 1820).

grammar.title: Must / have to (obligation)
grammar.form: must + verbo básico · have to / has to / had to + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Must expressa obrigação ou necessidade forte, muitas vezes vinda de quem fala: I must go. Have to expressa obrigação externa e é usado em todos os tempos: We had to wait. Mustn't significa proibição; don't have to significa que não é necessário.

grammar.title: Should / ought to (advice)
grammar.form: should + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para conselhos, opiniões e o que é correto fazer: You should rest. A man should keep his warmth inside him. Equivale a 'deveria'.

grammar.title: First conditional
grammar.form: If + presente simples, will + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para condições reais ou prováveis no futuro: If you go, I will follow you. If he finds it, I am lost. A oração com if pode vir antes ou depois.

grammar.title: Verb + to-infinitive / -ing
grammar.form: want/decide/try/begin/hope + to + verbo · enjoy/stop/finish/keep/like + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Alguns verbos são seguidos de to + verbo (He decided to go), outros de verbo-ing (She stopped crying). Alguns aceitam os dois, às vezes com sentidos diferentes (stop to talk = parar para conversar; stop talking = parar de conversar).

grammar.title: Passive voice
grammar.form: be (no tempo desejado) + particípio passado: is made, was killed, has been seen, will be found
grammar.explanation: Usada quando a ação é mais importante do que quem a pratica, ou quando não sabemos quem a praticou: The boat was broken in half. The ship was named after a tribe. Para dizer quem fez, use by: He was killed by a whale.

grammar.title: Past perfect
grammar.form: had + particípio passado
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que aconteceu antes de outra ação no passado: When we arrived, the ship had already left. Equivale ao 'tinha feito' do português. É muito comum em narrativas, para voltar no tempo.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.form: who (pessoas) · which (coisas) · that (pessoas ou coisas) · whose (posse) · where (lugar)
grammar.explanation: Dão informação sobre um substantivo: the man who sold heads; the boat which was broken; the woman whose son was lost. Who e that podem ser omitidos quando são objeto: the book (that) I read.

grammar.title: Reported speech
grammar.form: say / tell + (that) + oração, normalmente com o tempo verbal recuado: 'I am ill' → He said that he was ill.
grammar.explanation: Para contar o que alguém disse sem usar aspas. Os tempos costumam recuar um passo no passado (am → was, will → would, have seen → had seen). Use tell + pessoa (He told me...) e say sem pessoa (He said...).

grammar.title: Second conditional
grammar.form: If + passado simples, would + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para situações imaginárias ou improváveis no presente ou no futuro: If I had a gun, I would destroy him. Com o verbo to be, a forma formal é were para todas as pessoas: If I were you...

grammar.title: Used to
grammar.form: used to + verbo básico
grammar.explanation: Para hábitos ou estados do passado que não existem mais: We used to sit by the fire. Equivale a 'costumava'. Não confunda com be used to + -ing (estar acostumado a).

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
grammar.form: have / has been + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que começou no passado e continua até agora, com ênfase na duração: I have been waiting for hours. I have been thinking about it.

grammar.title: Past perfect continuous
grammar.form: had been + verbo-ing
grammar.explanation: Para uma ação que estava em andamento até um momento do passado: She had been crying when he arrived. Mostra duração antes de outro acontecimento passado.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction
grammar.form: must / might / may / could / can't + be ou + verbo
grammar.explanation: Para expressar certeza ou possibilidade sobre algo que deduzimos: It must be the Count (tenho quase certeza). He might be asleep (talvez). It can't be true (não é possível).

grammar.title: Third conditional
grammar.form: If + had + particípio, would have + particípio
grammar.explanation: Para imaginar um passado diferente do que aconteceu: If I had listened to him, none of this would have happened. Expressa arrependimento ou consequências que não aconteceram.

grammar.title: Wish
grammar.form: wish + passado (desejo sobre o presente) · wish + had + particípio (arrependimento sobre o passado)
grammar.explanation: I wish I were at home = eu gostaria de estar em casa (mas não estou). I wish I had never come here = eu queria nunca ter vindo (mas vim).

grammar.title: Modal + have + past participle
grammar.form: should have / could have / might have / must have + particípio
grammar.explanation: Para falar sobre o passado com dedução ou crítica: He must have been there (deve ter estado). You should have told me (deveria ter me contado). It might have been a dream (pode ter sido).

grammar.title: Phrasal verbs
grammar.form: verbo + partícula (up, down, out, off, on, in, back...)
grammar.explanation: Verbos combinados com uma partícula que muitas vezes muda o sentido: give up (desistir), find out (descobrir), wake up (acordar). Os mais comuns dos livros também aparecem na aba Vocabulário, em Expressões.
